Near-Optimal Constructive Bounds for ℓ2\ell_{2} Prefix Discrepancy and Steinitz Problems via Affine Spectral Independence

Kunal Dutta ††thanks: University of Warsaw, Warsaw, Poland. kdutta@mimuw.edu.pl. Supported by the Polish NCN OPUS grant nr. 2023/51/B/ST6/02989.    Agastya Vibhuti Jha ††thanks: University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA. agastyajha@uchicago.edu.    Haotian Jiang ††thanks: University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA. jhtdavid@uchicago.edu.

A classical result of Steinitz from 1913 [53], answering an earlier question of Riemann and Lévy (e.g., [43]), states that for any norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and any set of vectors v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying ∑i=1nvi=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}=0, there exists an ordering π:[n]→[n]\pi:[n]\rightarrow[n] such that every partial sum along this order is bounded by O⁡(d)O(d), i.e., ‖∑i=1tvπ⁡(i)‖≤O⁡(d)\big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}v_{\pi(i)}\big\|\leq O(d) for all t∈[n]t\in[n].

Steinitz’s bound is tight up to constants in general, but for the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2}, it has been conjectured that the best bound is O⁡(d)O(\sqrt{d}). Almost a century later, a breakthrough work of Banaszczyk [5] gave a bound of O⁡(d+log⁡n)O(\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{\log n}) for the ℓ2\ell_{2} Steinitz problem, matching the conjecture under the mild assumption that d≥Ω⁡(log⁡n)d\geq\Omega(\log n). Banaszczyk’s result is non-constructive, and the previous best algorithmic bound was O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(\sqrt{d\log n}), due to Bansal and Garg [8].

In this work, we give an efficient algorithm that matches the conjectured O⁡(d)O(\sqrt{d}) bound for the ℓ2\ell_{2} Steinitz problem under the slightly worse, yet still polylogarithmic, condition of d≥Ω⁡(log7⁡n)d\geq\Omega(\log^{7}n). As in prior work, our result extends to the harder problem of ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy.

We employ the framework of obtaining the desired ordering via a discrete Brownian motion, guided by a semidefinite program (SDP). To obtain our results, we use the new technique of “Decoupling via Affine Spectral Independence”, proposed by Bansal and Jiang [13] to achieve substantial progress on the Beck-Fiala and Komlós conjectures, together with a “Global Interval Tree” data structure that simultaneously controls the deviations for all prefixes.

1 Introduction

The Steinitz problem is a fundamental question in combinatorial discrepancy theory that studies how well one can control the discrepancy of partial sums of vectors under permutations. Formally, given a norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| and a set of vectors v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying ‖vi‖≤1\|v_{i}\|\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n]11 1 Throughout, we use [n][n] to denote the set {1,⋯,n}\{1,\cdots,n\}. and ∑i∈[n]vi=0\sum_{i\in[n]}v_{i}=0, the Steinitz problem asks for the smallest number S(∥⋅∥)S(\|\cdot\|), depending only on the norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|, such that there exists an ordering π:[n]→[n]\pi:[n]\rightarrow[n] for which all partial sums along this ordering are at most S(∥⋅∥)S(\|\cdot\|), i.e., maxt∈[n]∥∑i∈[t]vπ⁡(i)∥≤S(∥⋅∥)\max_{t\in[n]}\big\|\sum_{i\in[t]}v_{\pi(i)}\big\|\leq S(\|\cdot\|). This was originally a question of Riemann and Lévy [43] from the early 1900s, and it has later found many surprising applications in areas such as graph theory [1], integer programming [25, 30, 31, 40], and scheduling [21, 50]. We refer readers to the surveys [35, 50, 22] for more details on the history and applications of the Steinitz problem.

A classical result of Steinitz [53] showed that S(∥⋅∥)≤2dS(\|\cdot\|)\leq 2d, regardless of the norm. Subsequently, this bound was improved to 1.5​d1.5d in [21] and then further to slightly better than dd [34, 3]. In particular, the proof by Grinberg and Sevastyanov in [34] uses a clever iterated rounding argument, which also implies an efficient algorithm for finding a good ordering π\pi.

The above bound of O⁡(d)O(d) is the best possible up to constants for general norms, e.g., S(∥⋅∥1)≥d/2S(\|\cdot\|_{1})\geq d/2. But for the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm, the best lower bound is only S(∥⋅∥2)≥Ω(d)S(\|\cdot\|_{2})\geq\Omega(\sqrt{d}) [24, 34]. While no o⁡(d)o(d) bound is known for ℓ2\ell_{2}, it was conjectured that Θ⁡(d)\Theta(\sqrt{d}) should be the right answer.22 2 Note that one may assume d≤n2d\leq n^{2}, as otherwise the trivial discrepancy bound of nn already achieves the conjectured O⁡(d)O(\sqrt{d}) bound. We make the assumption d≤n2d\leq n^{2} throughout this work. In breakthrough work, Banaszczyk [5] proved that S(∥⋅∥2)≤O(d+log⁡n)S(\|\cdot\|_{2})\leq O(\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{\log n}), matching the conjectured bound up to constants under the mild assumption of d≥log⁡nd\geq\log n. Unlike the O⁡(d)O(d) bound above, Banaszczyk’s proof is non-constructive and does not give an efficient algorithm for finding a good ordering (we discuss more on algorithmic aspects of discrepancy theory in Section 1.3). On the algorithmic front, [38] gave a constructive proof of O⁡(d​log2.5​n)O(\sqrt{d}\log^{2.5}n), and the previous best algorithmic bound was O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(\sqrt{d\log n}) due to Bansal and Garg [8]. Unlike Banaszczyk’s result, these algorithmic bounds don’t match the conjectured bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} Steinitz in any regime, and it is a natural open question to algorithmically attain Banaszczyk’s bound for this problem (e.g., see [6]).

Prefix Discrepancy. A closely-related question is the ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy33 3 The prefix discrepancy problem is also referred to as the signed series problem in the literature. problem, introduced by Spencer [51]: given a sequence of vectors v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖vi‖2≤1\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], the goal is to find a coloring x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} so that the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of all partial signed sum is bounded by a number E(∥⋅∥2)E(\|\cdot\|_{2}), i.e., maxt∈[n]∥∑i=1txivt∥2≤E(∥⋅∥2)\max_{t\in[n]}\big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{t}\big\|_{2}\leq E(\|\cdot\|_{2}). Variants of this prefix problem have been well-studied and they have many applications to online algorithms [41, 10, 9, 2], Tusnády’s problem [47], and flow time scheduling [15].

For ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy, Spencer [51] showed a bound that only depends on dd. Using iterated rounding, Bárány and Grinberg [20] gave an algorithmic bound of 2​d−12d-1. Similar to ℓ2\ell_{2} Steinitz, it has been conjectured that the correct bound for E(∥⋅∥2)E(\|\cdot\|_{2}) should be Θ⁡(d)\Theta(\sqrt{d}). The ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy problem is actually known to be harder than the Steinitz problem — Chobanyan [28] gave a reduction between the two problems which shows that S(∥⋅∥2)≤E(∥⋅∥2)S(\|\cdot\|_{2})\leq E(\|\cdot\|_{2}), and this reduction can be made algorithmic [38]. In fact, both the non-constructive bound of O⁡(d+log⁡n)O(\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{\log n}) in [5] and the algorithmic bound of O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(\sqrt{d\log n}) in [8] above were given for the harder ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy problem and then they used this reduction as a black box.

1.1 Our Results

Our main result is an improved algorithmic bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy that matches the conjectured Θ⁡(d)\Theta(\sqrt{d}) bound under the slightly worse, yet still polylogarithmic, condition of d≥log7⁡nd\geq\log^{7}n (recall that in Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound, the condition was d≥log⁡nd\geq\log n).

Theorem 1.1.

(Algorithmic ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy) Given v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖vi‖2≤1\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], one can efficiently find x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that ‖∑i=1txi​vi‖2≤O⁡(d+d1/4​log7/4​n)\big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\big\|_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\log^{7/4}n) for all prefix t∈[n]t\in[n]. In particular, the bound matches the conjectured Θ⁡(d)\Theta(\sqrt{d}) when d≥log7⁡nd\geq\log^{7}n.

Unlike the constructive bound in [8] that loses a multiplicative O⁡(log⁡n)O(\sqrt{\log n}) factor, the bound in Theorem 1.1 (as well as the other results below) is only off from the conjectured bound by an additive factor, which is of lower order when d≥𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)d\geq\mathsf{polylog}(n). While not stated explicitly, our bounds are also never worse than those in [8], as our algorithms are built on top of theirs.

Using the algorithmic reduction in [28, 38] as a black box, Theorem 1.1 also implies the same algorithmic improvement for the ℓ2\ell_{2} Steinitz problem. This gets close to answering the question of algorithmically matching Banaszczyk’s bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} Steinitz in [6].

Corollary 1.2 (Algorithmic ℓ2\ell_{2} Steinitz).

Given vectors v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that ∑i=1nvi=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_{i}=0 and ‖vi‖2≤1\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], one can efficiently find a permutation π:[n]→[n]\pi:[n]\rightarrow[n] such that ‖∑i=1tvπ⁡(i)‖2≤O⁡(d+d1/4​log7/4​n)\big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}v_{\pi(i)}\big\|_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\log^{7/4}n) for all prefix t∈[n]t\in[n]. This bound matches the conjectured Θ⁡(d)\Theta(\sqrt{d}) bound when d≥log7⁡nd\geq\log^{7}n.

It is an intriguing open question to improve the condition of d≥log7⁡nd\geq\log^{7}n in Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 to get close to the condition of d≥log⁡nd\geq\log n in Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound [5]. We give such an improvement in the case where coordinates of the vectors viv_{i} are “well-spread”, namely, each coordinate of every viv_{i} has magnitude at most 1/d1/\sqrt{d}. Equivalently, one may scale the vectors v1,⋯,vnv_{1},\cdots,v_{n} up by a d\sqrt{d} factor and assume that each viv_{i} satisfies ‖vi‖∞≤1\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1. Under this scaling, the conjectured bound becomes Θ⁡(d)\Theta(d), where the lower bound is witnessed by a Hadamard matrix. The previous best constructive bound for this setting was O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(d\sqrt{\log n}) by Bansal and Garg [8].

Theorem 1.3.

(Algorithmic ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy) Given v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖vi‖∞≤1\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], one can efficiently find x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that ‖∑i=1txi​vi‖2≤O⁡(d+d3/4​log⁡n+d1/4​log3/2​n)\big\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\big\|_{2}\leq O(d+d^{3/4}\log n+d^{1/4}\log^{3/2}n) for all prefix t∈[n]t\in[n]. This matches the conjectured Θ⁡(d)\Theta(d) bound when d≥log4⁡nd\geq\log^{4}n.

1.2 Our Approach in a Nutshell

We view the given vectors v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} as a matrix A∈ℝd×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} whose jjth column is vjv_{j}. Denote by Ai∈ℝnA_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} its iith row. Throughout, we use v⁡(ℓ)v(\ell) to denote the ℓ\ellth entry of a vector vv and log\log means logarithm to the base 22. We always use i∈[d]i\in[d] to index rows of AA, and j∈[n]j\in[n] for columns, and use 𝒫⊆[n]\mathcal{P}\subseteq[n] to denote an arbitrary prefix whose discrepancy we will bound.

Similar to prior works, our algorithm starts with x0=0nx_{0}=0^{n} and evolves a fractional coloring xt∈[−1,1]nx_{t}\in[-1,1]^{n} using carefully chosen random tiny increments Δ​xt\Delta x_{t}. As in [8], to handle all prefixes, our algorithm maintains a sliding window Wt⊆[n]W_{t}\subseteq[n] containing the first 10​d10d alive columns jj for which xt​(j)x_{t}(j) has not yet reached ±1\pm 1, and ensures that (1) Δ​xt\Delta x_{t} is supported only on WtW_{t}, and (2) the discrepancy update of the full sliding window is 00, i.e., ∑j∈WtAi​(j)​Δ​xt​(j)=0\sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)\Delta x_{t}(j)=0 for every row i∈[d]i\in[d]. This guarantees that each prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n] only incurs non-zero discrepancy while 𝒫∈Wt\mathcal{P}\in W_{t}.

Roughly speaking, prior algorithms [7, 8, 14] choose the increment Δ​xt\Delta x_{t} to be O⁡(1)O(1)-spectrally independent, which ensures that the discrepancy φt𝒫​(i)\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) for each prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n] and each row i∈[d]i\in[d] is O⁡(d)O(d)-subgaussian.44 4 A mean-zero random vector φ∈ℝm\varphi\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is called σ2\sigma^{2}-subgaussian, if for any unit test vector θ∈ℝm\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, it satisfies the Gaussian-type tail bound Pr(|⟨θ,φ⟩|≥t)≤2exp(−t2/(2σ2))\Pr(|\langle\theta,\varphi\rangle|\geq t)\leq 2\exp(-t^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})). This suffices for Bansal-Garg’s O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(d\sqrt{\log n}) bound for ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy — subgaussianity ensures that each row prefix discrepancy |φt𝒫​(i)|≤O⁡(d​log⁡n)|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)|\leq O(\sqrt{d\log n}) with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), which implies ‖φt𝒫‖2≤O⁡(d​log⁡n)\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq O(d\sqrt{\log n}) by taking a union bound over all rows i∈[d]i\in[d] and prefixes 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n]. A similar argument can also recover55 5 The original proof of the ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy bound in [8] was done by analyzing the dynamics of d​‖φt𝒫‖22d\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}^{2}, but a row-wise analysis already recovers their bound and is technically slightly simpler. Bansal-Garg’s bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy, but we will focus on the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2} setting here for simplicity.

The main bottleneck for Bansal-Garg’s bound is that while each φt𝒫​(i)\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) is O⁡(d)O(d)-subgaussian, they may have arbitrarily correlations, and this is why a row-wise analysis is needed to control φt𝒫​(i)\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) up to a 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/\mathsf{poly}(n) tail probability (and hence loses a O⁡(log⁡n)O(\sqrt{\log n}) multiplicative factor) to union bound over all rows and prefixes. To avoid this loss, we observe that if the φt𝒫​(i)\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) were mutually independent, standard concentration inequalities would give an additive deviation, and recover Banaszczyk’s non-constructive O⁡(d+d​log⁡n)O(d+\sqrt{d\log n}) bound. Although it is clearly impossible to achieve full independence for φt𝒫​(i)\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i), we leverage the recent technique of “Decoupling via Affine Spectral Independence” in [13] to ensure that the change in prefix discrepancy Δ​φt𝒫​(i)\Delta\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) is affine spectrally independent — this weaker form of independence turns out to be sufficient for an additive ℓ2\ell_{2} discrepancy bound on φt𝒫\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}, albeit with a worse additive term (than the fully independent case).

Nonetheless, the use of affine spectral independence posts a technical challenge — the independence degrades as one controls more rows/prefixes. Naively, at each time tt, one needs to control dd rows for each of the |Wt|=10​d|W_{t}|=10d prefixes in the sliding window, but including all these Θ⁡(d2)\Theta(d^{2}) row-prefix pairs would result in too weak of an independence to even improve upon the Bansal-Garg bound. To bypass this issue, we only enforce affine spectral independence for a carefully chosen set of o⁡(d)o(d) prefixes in WtW_{t} called ASI-guarded prefixes. To maintain this set of ASI-guarded prefixes dynamically and to bound the discrepancies of the remaining unguarded prefixes, we design a Global Interval Tree data structure to simultaneously control their additive deviations.

Roadmap. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Some further related work will be discussed in Section 1.3. We then give an overview of our approach in Section 2. A formal presentation of our algorithmic framework, data structure, and meta analysis will appear in Section 3. Then in Section 4, we prove our result for ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy in Theorem 1.3. Finally, we prove our ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy bound in Theorem 1.1 in Section 5. We will conclude and mention some open problems in Section 6. Some missing details will be given in the appendix.

1.3 Further Related Work

Combinatorial Discrepancy. Combinatorial discrepancy theory is a well-studied topic with many connections and applications to both mathematics and computer science, and we refer readers to the textbooks [26, 46, 27]. A classical question in combinatorial discrepancy is the following vector balancing problem: given a norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| and vectors v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the goal is to find a coloring x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} to minimize 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼∥⋅∥(v1,⋯,vn):=minx∈{±1}n∥∑i=1nxivi∥\mathsf{disc}_{\|\cdot\|}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n}):=\min_{x\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\big\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}v_{i}\big\|. This question is easier than prefix discrepancy, as one only bounds the total signed sum. For instance, for the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm, a classical result of Bárány and Grinberg [20] shows that 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼∥⋅∥2(v1,⋯,vn)≤O(d)\mathsf{disc}_{\|\cdot\|_{2}}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n})\leq O(\sqrt{d}) when each ‖vi‖2≤1\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 and this bound is tight up to constants.

ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} Discrepancy and Algorithmic Aspects. While our focus here is on ℓ2\ell_{2} discrepancy, we remark that ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} discrepancy is also very natural, and its study has led to many interesting techniques and developments in discrepancy theory. A seminal result of Spencer [52] (and independently, Gluskin [33]) shows that if each ‖vi‖∞≤1\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1 and d=nd=n, then 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼∥⋅∥∞(v1,⋯,vn)≤O(n)\mathsf{disc}_{\|\cdot\|_{\infty}}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n})\leq O(\sqrt{n}). This beats the O⁡(n​log⁡n)O(\sqrt{n\log n}) bound for a random coloring, and is optimal up to constants.

When each ‖vi‖2≤1\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1, the long-standing Komlós conjecture, generalizing a seminal conjecture of Beck and Fiala [23], asserts that 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝖼∥⋅∥∞(v1,⋯,vn)≤O(1)\mathsf{disc}_{\|\cdot\|_{\infty}}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{n})\leq O(1). For the Komlós problem, Spencer [52] gave an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) bound. This was improved to O⁡(log⁡n)O(\sqrt{\log n}) by Banaszczyk [4]. His results for prefix discrepancy and Steinitz problems in [5] are crucially based on this earlier work.

While the above approaches for ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} discrepancy have become prominent in discrepancy theory, these methods were originally non-constructive and did not give an efficient algorithm for finding a good coloring. Following a breakthrough of Bansal [17], many elegant algorithms have been developed that matches these non-constructive bounds [16, 37, 44, 29, 49, 42, 32, 6, 7, 2, 14, 39, 48, 36, 12], leading to surprising applications in many different areas (e.g., see the excellent survey [18]). Interestingly, they also provide new insights into discrepancy theory and lately, building on top of these algorithmic developments, Bansal and Jiang [11, 13] gave an improved O⁡((log1/4⁡n)⋅𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(log⁡log⁡n))O((\log^{1/4}n)\cdot\mathsf{poly}(\log\log n)) bound for the Komlós problem and almost resolved the Beck-Fiala conjecture.

ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} Prefix Discrepancy. The ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy problem, where the objective is to bound maxt∈[n]⁡‖∑i=1txi​vi‖∞\max_{t\in[n]}\|\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\|_{\infty}, is also well-studied. When each ‖vi‖∞≤1\|v_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1, it was conjectured that the correct bound should be Θ⁡(d)\Theta(\sqrt{d}). Banaszczyk [5] gave a non-constructive bound of O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(\sqrt{d\log n}), and this bound was later matched algorithmically in [8].

The case where each ‖vi‖2≤1\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq 1 (i.e., the prefix version of Komlós problem) is more elusive. The best non-constructive bound is O⁡(log⁡n)O(\sqrt{\log n}) [5], while the best algorithmic bound is only O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) [2]. It was asked in [9] whether the Komlós conjecture generalizes to this prefix setting, i.e., whether the best bound is O⁡(1)O(1), but there is no clear consensus on this question.

2 Overview of Our Approach

In this section, we give an overview of our approach. Our focus here will be on the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy bound in Theorem 1.3, since it is technically simpler (than ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy) but already contains most of the ideas. We start with the algorithmic framework that we will use throughout the paper. Here we adopt the same notation as in Section 1.2.

2.1 Algorithmic Framework: SDP-Guided Walk with A Sliding Window

As in many previous discrepancy algorithms [8, 7, 14, 19, 11, 13], our algorithms start with x0=0nx_{0}=0^{n}, and evolve a fractional coloring xt∈[−1,1]nx_{t}\in[-1,1]^{n} over time using tiny random increments, until some final coloring in {±1}n\{\pm 1\}^{n} is reached. The time tt will range from 00 to nn, and is updated in discrete increments of size d​tdt. We will set d​t=1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)dt=1/\mathsf{poly}(n) so that the algorithm runs in polynomial time, but it is useful to view d​tdt as infinitesimally small.

Sliding Window and Coloring Update. At each time tt, a column j∈[n]j\in[n] is alive if |xt​(j)|≤1−1/(2​n​d)|x_{t}(j)|\leq 1-1/(2nd), and is called dead otherwise. Notice that rounding a dead column to either 11 or −1-1 incurs a negligible O⁡(1/(n​d))O(1/(nd)) discrepancy per column, and thus will be ignored henceforth. Let Wt⊆[n]W_{t}\subseteq[n] be the first 10​d10d alive columns, which we will refer to as the sliding window. The columns in WtW_{t} will be called active, and alive columns not contained in WtW_{t} are called dormant. The algorithm will only update the coloring xt​(j)x_{t}(j) for j∈Wtj\in W_{t}, and ensures that the discrepancy update of the whole sliding window is 00.

Specifically, at time tt, the algorithm chooses a random vector ut∈ℝWtu_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} satisfying 𝔼⁡[ut]=0\mathbb{E}[u_{t}]=0, ‖ut‖2=1\|u_{t}\|_{2}=1, xt⟂utx_{t}\perp u_{t}, and ∑j∈WtAi​(j)​ut​(j)=0\sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0 for all rows i∈[d]i\in[d] (and various other properties that will be specified later).66 6 We sometimes abuse notation and also view utu_{t} as a vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with ut​(j)=0u_{t}(j)=0 for all j∉Wtj\notin W_{t}. The coloring xtx_{t} is updated to xt+d​t=xt+d​xtx_{t+dt}=x_{t}+dx_{t} with

d​xt=ut​d​t.dx_{t}=u_{t}\sqrt{dt}.

Note that ‖ut‖2=1\|u_{t}\|_{2}=1 and xt⟂utx_{t}\perp u_{t} ensures that ‖xt‖22=t\|x_{t}\|_{2}^{2}=t for all tt, so the process ends by t=nt=n. Also notice that ∑j∈WtAi​(j)​ut​(j)=0\sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0 for all i∈[d]i\in[d] ensures that the sliding window incurs 00 discrepancy change, and thus any prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n] only incurs non-zero discrepancy when 𝒫∈Wt\mathcal{P}\in W_{t}.

Choosing utu_{t} via an SDP. The power of this framework comes from the flexibility to choose utu_{t} adaptively at each time tt. To do this, the algorithm computes a PSD matrix UtU_{t} by solving a semidefinite program (SDP), and samples utu_{t} with UtU_{t} as the covariance matrix. As this approach of sampling utu_{t} via solving an SDP is already standard, to simplify the discussion here, we postpone the details of the SDP and how to sample utu_{t} from UtU_{t} to Section 3.

2.2 Spectral Independence and the Bansal-Garg Bound

A useful property ensured by the SDP in prior algorithms is that utu_{t} is O⁡(1)O(1)-spectrally independent:

𝖢𝗈𝗏⁡(ut)⪯O⁡(1)⋅𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀⁡(𝖢𝗈𝗏⁡(ut)).\displaystyle\mathsf{Cov}(u_{t})\preceq O(1)\cdot\mathsf{diag}(\mathsf{Cov}(u_{t})). (𝖲𝖨\mathsf{SI})

Since 𝖢𝗈𝗏⁡(ut)=𝔼⁡[ut​ut⊤]\mathsf{Cov}(u_{t})=\mathbb{E}[u_{t}u_{t}^{\top}] for mean-zero utu_{t}, this is equivalent to saying that for any vector a∈ℝWta\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}},

𝔼⁡[⟨a,ut⟩2]=𝔼⁡[(∑j∈Wta⁡(j)​ut​(j))2]≤O⁡(1)⋅∑j∈Wta​(j)2​ut​(j)2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\langle a,u_{t}\rangle^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\sum_{j\in W_{t}}a(j)u_{t}(j)\big)^{2}\Big]\leq O(1)\cdot\sum_{j\in W_{t}}a(j)^{2}u_{t}(j)^{2}, (1)

which intuitively means that the coordinates of utu_{t} is almost pairwise independent (up to a constant factor loss). Surprisingly, this seemingly weak form of independence implies strong subgaussian-type concentration for discrepancy in the algorithmic framework above [7, 8]. In particular, if utu_{t} is O⁡(1)O(1)-spectrally independent for all time tt, then for any test vector a∈ℝna\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, its discrepancy change over any time period [t1,t2][t_{1},t_{2}] is essentially O⁡(‖a‖2)O(\|a\|_{2})-subgaussian, i.e.,

Pr⁡(|⟨a,xt2−xt1⟩|≥c⋅‖a‖2)≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(c2)).\displaystyle\Pr(|\langle a,x_{t_{2}}-x_{t_{1}}\rangle|\geq c\cdot\|a\|_{2})\leq\exp(-\Omega(c^{2})). (2)

The Bansal-Garg Bound. The tail bound in (2) turns out to be sufficient to recover Bansal and Garg’s results in [8]. Here, we show their O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(d\sqrt{\log n}) bound for ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy (their O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(\sqrt{d\log n}) bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy follows from a similar argument). Recall that Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound is O⁡(d+d​log⁡n)O(d+\sqrt{d\log n}) in the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2} setting.

Fix a prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n]. Denote Ai𝒫∈[−1,1]𝒫A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\in[-1,1]^{\mathcal{P}} the row AiA_{i} restricted to the prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and denote φt𝒫​(i)=⟨Ai𝒫,xt⟩\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=\langle A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}},x_{t}\rangle the discrepancy of row ii for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P}. We will show that with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), |φn𝒫​(i)|≤O⁡(d​log⁡n)|\varphi^{\mathcal{P}}_{n}(i)|\leq O(\sqrt{d\log n}) for all row i∈[d]i\in[d], which implies that ‖φn𝒫‖2≤O⁡(d​log⁡n)\|\varphi^{\mathcal{P}}_{n}\|_{2}\leq O(d\sqrt{\log n}). Taking a union bound over all prefixes 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n] then gives the Bansal-Garg result.

To bound φn𝒫​(i)\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i), let t∗t^{*} be the first time when column 𝒫\mathcal{P} enters the sliding window, and let ai𝒫∈ℝWt∗a_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t^{*}}} be the vector Ai𝒫A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}} restricted to that particular sliding window Wt∗W_{t^{*}}. Clearly, we have ‖ai𝒫‖2≤10​d\|a_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{10d} as the sliding window only has 10​d10d alive columns. Since prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} does not incur any discrepancy before it enters the sliding window, we have φt∗𝒫​(i)=0\varphi_{t^{*}}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=0. Note that only the coloring update of columns in Wt∗W_{t^{*}} can contribute to φt𝒫\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} after time t∗t^{*}, and thus φn𝒫​(i)=⟨ai𝒫,xn−xt∗⟩\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=\langle a_{i}^{\mathcal{P}},x_{n}-x_{t^{*}}\rangle. Then using (2) with c=O⁡(log⁡n)c=O(\sqrt{\log n}) for large enough constants and ‖ai𝒫‖2≤O⁡(d)\|a_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d}) gives the desired bound

Pr⁡(|φn𝒫​(i)|≥O⁡(d​log⁡n))≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(c2))=1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n).\Pr(|\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)|\geq O(\sqrt{d\log n}))\leq\exp(-\Omega(c^{2}))=1/\mathsf{poly}(n).

Where Can We Improve? The main reason for the O⁡(log⁡n)O(\sqrt{\log n}) factor loss in the Bansal-Garg bound is the following. Although each φn𝒫​(i)\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) is O⁡(d)O(d)-subgaussian, the different φn𝒫​(i)\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)’s may have arbitrary correlations, so they need to bound each φn𝒫​(i)\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) up to a tail probability of 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/\mathsf{poly}(n) to take a union bound over all rows i∈[d]i\in[d] and prefixes 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n]. This row-wise analysis is generally the best possible without any additional control over the correlations among the φn𝒫​(i)\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)’s.

However, in an ideal scenario where the discrepancies of all rows φn𝒫​(i)\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) are evolving independently, standard concentration inequalities (e.g., see [54, Theorem 3.1.1]) give the following stronger tail bound for ‖φn𝒫‖2\|\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2} (than the row-wise analysis above) with an additive deviation:

Pr⁡(‖φn𝒫‖2≥O⁡(d​(d+c)))≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(c2)).\displaystyle\Pr\big(\|\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\geq O(\sqrt{d}(\sqrt{d}+c))\big)\leq\exp(-\Omega(c^{2})).

Taking c=O⁡(log⁡n)c=O(\sqrt{\log n}) here allows for a union bound over all prefixes 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n], and this would already recover Banaszczyk’s non-constructive O⁡(d+d​log⁡n)O(d+\sqrt{d\log n}) result.

Of course, as the discrepancies φn𝒫​(i)\varphi_{n}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) of different rows i∈[d]i\in[d] are generated by the same dynamics d​xtdx_{t}, it is not realistic to assume that they are independent. Nonetheless, this dependency among row discrepancies is exactly the issue encountered by Bansal and Jiang [11, 13] when studying the Beck-Fiala and Komlós conjectures. To bypass the issue and achieve substantial progress towards these long-standing conjectures, they devised a new technique to “decouple” the discrepancies of different rows using a new set of SDP constraints for utu_{t} called affine spectral independence.

2.3 Affine Spectral Independence and ASI-Guarded Prefixes

The idea in [13] is to add a new set of affine spectral independence (ASI) constraints to the SDP to ensure that d​φt𝒫=φt+d​t𝒫−φt𝒫d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}=\varphi_{t+dt}^{\mathcal{P}}-\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} is γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}-spectrally independent (see Section 3 for details), i.e.,

𝖢𝗈𝗏⁡(d​φt𝒫)⪯γ𝖠𝖲𝖨⋅𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀⁡(𝖢𝗈𝗏⁡(d​φt𝒫)).\displaystyle\mathsf{Cov}(d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}})\preceq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot\mathsf{diag}(\mathsf{Cov}(d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}})). (𝖠𝖲𝖨\mathsf{ASI})

Similar to (1), this intuitively says that the discrepancy change d​φt𝒫​(i)d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) of different rows i∈[d]i\in[d] are almost pairwise independent up to a γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} factor, and we show that this weaker form of independence suffices for an additive bound. In particular, we analyze the dynamics of d​‖φt𝒫‖22d\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}^{2} as in [8],

d​‖φt𝒫‖22=2​⟨φt𝒫,d​φt𝒫⟩⏟d​Lt𝒫+⟨d​φt𝒫,d​φt𝒫⟩⏟d​Qt𝒫.d\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}^{2}=2\underbrace{\langle\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}},d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rangle}_{dL^{\mathcal{P}}_{t}}+\underbrace{\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}},d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rangle}_{dQ^{\mathcal{P}}_{t}}.

[8] already gave a bound for the quadratic term Qt𝒫Q_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} matching Banaszczyk’s bound, using ( SI ) and a Freedman-type martingale analysis (see Section 3.3), and the main bottleneck there lies in controlling the linear term Lt𝒫L_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}. It turns out that the ( ASI ) property reduces the quadratic variation of Lt𝒫L_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}, which allows us to show that with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),

‖φt𝒫‖2≤O⁡(d+γ𝖠𝖲𝖨⋅d​log⁡n).\displaystyle\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq O(d+\sqrt{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot d\log n}). (3)

We defer the technical details to Section 4, but this essentially recovers Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound if the ASI factor γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} could be set to O⁡(1)O(1) as in the spectral independence property ( SI ).

Controlling All Prefixes Blows Up the ASI Factor. Unfortunately, while we can indeed set γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=O⁡(1)\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=O(1) in ( ASI ) for a fixed prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P}, a crucial issue arises when controlling multiple prefixes — the γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} factor suffers from the number of prefixes one needs to control simultaneously [13]. As the sliding window WtW_{t} has size 10​d10d, naively satisfying ( ASI ) for all prefixes 𝒫∈Wt\mathcal{P}\in W_{t} would result in setting γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=Θ⁡(d)\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=\Theta(d), for which the bound in (3) is no better than the Bansal-Garg bound.

To bypass this issue, we control a carefully chosen set of o⁡(d)o(d) prefixes ℐt⊆Wt\mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t} that we call ASI-guarded prefixes — this allows us to choose γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=|ℐt|=o⁡(d)\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=|\mathcal{I}_{t}|=o(d) (and we will think of γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=|ℐt|\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=|\mathcal{I}_{t}| henceforth), for which the bound in (3) improves upon Bansal-Garg. However, this forces us to lose the ( ASI ) control over most prefixes (i.e., those that are not ASI-guarded, which we will refer to as unguarded prefixes), and this poses two further technical challenges:

  1. (i)

    As the sliding window WtW_{t} evolves over time, we need to update the set of o⁡(d)o(d) many ASI-guarded prefixes dynamically.

  2. (ii)

    We need to control the discrepancies of all the 10​d−o⁡(d)10d-o(d) unguarded prefixes. In particular, some of the previous ASI-guarded prefixes might become unguarded later on, and we can no longer rely on (3) to bound their discrepancies.

To get around these challenges, we design a data structure for maintaining the set of o⁡(d)o(d) ASI-guarded prefixes that we call Global Interval Tree (and denoted as 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}).

2.4 Global Interval Tree: Controlling Unguarded Prefixes

In this subsection, we give an overview of the 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure and discuss how it overcomes the above challenges (see Sections 3.2 and 3.3 for more details).

The Interval Representation. Denote ℐt⊆Wt\mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t} the set of γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=o⁡(d)\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=o(d) ASI-guarded prefixes that 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} maintains at each time tt. Note that ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} naturally corresponds to a collection of consecutive intervals in [n][n], where each pair of adjacent ASI-guarded prefixes 𝒫1,𝒫2∈ℐt\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2}\in\mathcal{I}_{t} induces the interval (𝒫1,𝒫2]:={𝒫1+1,𝒫1+2,⋯,𝒫2}(\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2}]:=\{\mathcal{P}_{1}+1,\mathcal{P}_{1}+2,\cdots,\mathcal{P}_{2}\}. This collection of consecutive intervals essentially forms a partition (except for a final interval between max⁡{ℐt}\max\{\mathcal{I}_{t}\} and max⁡{Wt}\max\{W_{t}\}) of the columns in [Wt][W_{t}], where we use [Wt]:=[min⁡{Wt},max⁡{Wt}][W_{t}]:=[\min\{W_{t}\},\max\{W_{t}\}] to denote the set of all columns, alive or dead, that lies inside the range of the current sliding window WtW_{t}. We refer to [Wt][W_{t}] as the complete sliding window, and note that WtW_{t} only contains all the alive columns in [Wt][W_{t}].

From this interval perspective, an equivalent task is to maintain a set of o⁡(d)o(d) intervals that partition [Wt][W_{t}], which we abuse notation and also denote as ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}.

As the sliding window WtW_{t} progresses over time, the set of intervals ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} needs to be updated dynamically. For our purposes, we will perform two operations:

(1) add new intervals into ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} when new columns enter [Wt][W_{t}], and (2) merge consecutive intervals in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} when their sizes, i.e., the number of alive columns they currently contain, become too small (and thus too expensive to maintain separately).77 7 Note that merging two consecutive intervals corresponds to unguarding the ASI-guarded prefix between them.

Adding and Merging Intervals. To describe these operations formally, we partition [n][n] into n/sn/s base intervals of size s=ω⁡(1)s=\omega(1) each at time 00, and use ℬ\mathcal{B} to denote this collection of base intervals. We call a base interval I∈ℬI\in\mathcal{B} active at time tt if I⊆[1,max⁡{Wt}]I\subseteq[1,\max\{W_{t}\}] and I∩Wt≠∅I\cap W_{t}\neq\emptyset, i.e., when II contains at least one active column and no column in II is dormant. At time 00, the initial sliding window W0W_{0} (as well as ℐ0\mathcal{I}_{0}) contains the first 10​d/s=o⁡(d)10d/s=o(d) base intervals. We add a base interval I∈ℬI\in\mathcal{B} to ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} whenever it becomes active, and we will only add base intervals to ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} throughout.

An interval I∈ℐtI\in\mathcal{I}_{t} is said to be small if its size is at most s/2s/2. Ideally, we would like to merge two consecutive intervals when both of them are small to ensure that there are no small intervals, but we will need to do this carefully — as we will see in the following discussion, merging an interval too many times may blow up the discrepancy of the prefixes it contains.

Two Conflicting Goals. Before describing our merging strategy, we first address the challenges mentioned towards the end of Section 2.3. For challenge (i), the total number of intervals in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} must be o⁡(d)o(d), which is equivalent to the average size of intervals in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} being ω⁡(1)\omega(1):

Goal (i): the average interval size in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} should be ω⁡(1)\omega(1).

To control the discrepancy of an unguarded prefix 𝒫∈[Wt]\mathcal{P}\in[W_{t}] as posted in challenge (ii), let I∈ℐtI\in\mathcal{I}_{t} be the interval containing 𝒫\mathcal{P}. The left endpoint of II is an ASI-guarded prefix which we will call the ASI-guard for 𝒫\mathcal{P} at time tt. From this perspective, the discrepancy change for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} can be decomposed as d​φt𝒫=d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨+d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}, where d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} is the discrepancy change of its ASI-guard, and d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} is the discrepancy change of the (alive) columns between the ASI-guard and 𝒫\mathcal{P}, which we will refer to as the error columns or the error set (see Figure 3 for an illustration).

Roughly speaking, we will show (see Section 3.3 for details) that the contribution from the ASI-guard part d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} can still be bounded as in (3), even though the ASI-guard for 𝒫\mathcal{P} might change over time — thus as long as goal (i) is achieved, one has γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=|ℐt|=o⁡(d)\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=|\mathcal{I}_{t}|=o(d) and this suffices for bounding the ASI-guard part φt𝖠𝖲𝖨\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} better than the Bansal-Garg bound.

However, the discrepancy contribution of the error part d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} depends on the total number of columns that have ever been part of the error set for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} at any time — it can be bounded by O⁡((total # of error columns)⋅log⁡n)O(\sqrt{(\text{total \# of error columns})\cdot\log n}) using the Freedman-type martingale analysis in [8]. Note that the total number of error columns for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} depends on how many times the interval II containing 𝒫\mathcal{P} merges with the interval on its left (see Figure 4), and can be upper bounded by

(total # of times interval containing 𝒫 merges)⋅(s/2),(\text{total \# of times interval containing $\mathcal{P}$ merges})\cdot(s/2),

where recall that s/2s/2 is the threshold size for a small interval. This leads to the following goal:

Goal (ii): for every prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P}, the number of times the interval containing it merges is small.

Note that there is an obvious tension between the two goals above — avoiding small-sized intervals as in goal (i) naturally leads to substantial number of merges — but we will be able to achieve both goals using the strategy of merging via a global binary tree.

Merging via a Global Binary Tree. At time 00, we view the n/sn/s base intervals as the leaves of a complete global binary tree 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0}, whose depth is log⁡(n/s)=O⁡(log⁡n)\log(n/s)=O(\log n) (here we pretend that n/sn/s is a power of 22 for simplicity). At each time tt, we maintain 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} to be a subtree of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0}, such that the leaf nodes of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} (restricted to [Wt][W_{t}]) correspond to all the intervals maintained in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}.

Roughly speaking, when two base intervals corresponding to sibling leaves in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0} are both small, we will merge them into a single interval represented by their parent (and delete the two sibling leaves from 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0}). More generally, our rule for merging intervals is the following:88 8 For technical reasons, the actual merging rule that we use is slightly more sophisticated (see Merging Rule 3.3).

Merging Rule: Whenever two consecutive intervals I1,I2∈ℐtI_{1},I_{2}\in\mathcal{I}_{t} are both small at time tt and they correspond to the two sibling children of a parent node I0∈𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾tI_{0}\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, we will merge I1I_{1} and I2I_{2} into an interval for I0I_{0}, and delete the two sibling children from 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t}.

We will show that this merging rule ensures that each node only merges at most O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) times as the depth of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0} is O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), while at the same time, the average interval size is at least Ω⁡(s/log⁡n)\Omega(s/\log n). Setting s=ω⁡(1)s=\omega(1) properly then achieves our two goals above. See Section 3.2 for details.

3 Preliminaries and Our Framework

In this section, we formally describe our algorithmic framework and the meta-analysis that we use to achieve our results. We start with some notation.

Notation. As in Section 1.2, we view the vectors v1,⋯,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\cdots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} as a matrix A∈ℝd×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} whose jjth column is vjv_{j}, and use Ai∈ℝnA_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} to denote its iith row. For any W⊆[n]W\subseteq[n], denote Ai​(W)∈ℝWA_{i}(W)\in\mathbb{R}^{W} the row AiA_{i} restricted to columns in WW; for a vector u∈ℝWu\in\mathbb{R}^{W}, we sometimes abuse notation and view it as a vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with all-zero coordinates in [n]∖W[n]\setminus W. For any prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n], define A𝒫∈ℝd×𝒫A^{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times\mathcal{P}} (resp. Ai𝒫∈ℝ𝒫A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{P}}) as the matrix AA (resp. row AiA_{i}) restricted to the columns in prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

We use φ\varphi for discrepancy, and φt𝒫\varphi^{\mathcal{P}}_{t} to denote the discrepancy vector for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} at time tt. We always use i∈[d]i\in[d] to index rows of AA, and j∈[n]j\in[n] to index its columns.

Throughout, v⁡(ℓ)v(\ell) is the ℓ\ellth entry of vector vv and log\log means logarithm to the base 22.

We write ≲\lesssim (resp. ≳\gtrsim) when the left-hand side is at most (resp. at least) a constant times the right-hand side.

We define a notion of intervals for subsets of [n][n]. An interval in [n][n] is a consecutive set of elements in [n][n]. For ℓ,r∈[n]\ell,r\in[n] with ℓ≤r\ell\leq r, we denote [ℓ,r]:={ℓ,⋯,r}[\ell,r]:=\{\ell,\cdots,r\}, (ℓ,r]:={ℓ+1,⋯,r}(\ell,r]:=\{\ell+1,\cdots,r\}, [ℓ,r)={ℓ,⋯,r−1}[\ell,r)=\{\ell,\cdots,r-1\} the closed, left-open, and right-open intervals with boundaries ℓ\ell and rr. For a set W⊆[n]W\subseteq[n], we denote [W]:=[minℓ∈W⁡{ℓ},maxℓ∈W⁡{ℓ}][W]:=[\min_{\ell\in W}\{\ell\},\max_{\ell\in W}\{\ell\}] the smallest interval containing WW.

3.1 Algorithmic Framework: the SDP and Coloring Update

As described in Section 2.1, our algorithms find the desired coloring by evolving a fractional coloring xt∈[−1,1]nx_{t}\in[-1,1]^{n}, with x0=0nx_{0}=0^{n}, over time tt that increments in tiny steps of size d​t=1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)dt=1/\mathsf{poly}(n). The fractional coloring xtx_{t} is updated as d​xt=ut​d​tdx_{t}=u_{t}\sqrt{dt}, where ut∈ℝWtu_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} is a carefully-chosen random unit vector supported on the sliding window Wt⊆[n]W_{t}\subseteq[n] consisting of the first 10​d10d alive columns,99 9 If there are less than 10​d10d alive columns left, the sliding window WtW_{t} will contain all the remaining alive columns. This will happen after WtW_{t} hits the last column of the input matrix AA, and in this case, we will not enforce the constraint ∑j∈WtAi​(j)​ut​(j)=0\sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0 for any row i∈[d]i\in[d]. None of our analysis will be affected by this change of the size |Wt||W_{t}| at the end of the algorithm, and we will ignore this nuance throughout for simplicity.

so that |Wt|=10​d|W_{t}|=10d. In particular, utu_{t} will be chosen so that ut⟂xtu_{t}\perp x_{t} and that the discrepancy change of the whole sliding window WtW_{t} is 00, i.e., ∑j∈WtAi​(j)​ut​(j)=0\sum_{j\in W_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)=0 for all rows i∈[d]i\in[d].

As mentioned earlier, to choose utu_{t} at each time tt, our algorithms first computes a PSD matrix Ut∈ℝWt×WtU_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}\times W_{t}} by solving an SDP, and then samples utu_{t} with UtU_{t} as its covariance matrix (up to a constant scaling factor so that ‖ut‖2=1\|u_{t}\|_{2}=1). We first describe this SDP below and then explain the intuition behind its constraints. In prior works, this SDP has a few more parameters, but here we hard-code most of them to be constants to simplify our presentation.

Spreadness, Sliding Window, and Blocking Constraints. The first four constraints are standard and easy to parse. Constraints (4a) and (4b) ensures that the coloring update utu_{t} “uniformly spreads out” among its coordinates, and avoids the trivial solution U=0U=0. In particular, our algorithm always chooses xt∈Htx_{t}\in H_{t} to ensure that ut⟂xtu_{t}\perp x_{t}, as promised earlier.

Spectral Independence and Affine Spectral Independence. Corresponding to ( SI ), the spectral independence constraint (4e SI) guarantees that the random coloring update vector utu_{t} is 1010-spectrally independent. As explained in Section 2.2, this intuitively says that the coordinates of utu_{t} is almost pairwise independent up to a constant factor.

Analogously, corresponding to ( ASI ), the affine spectral independence constraint (4f ASI) guarantees that the discrepancy update d​φt𝒫d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} is γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}-spectrally independent for all ASI-guarded prefixes 𝒫∈ℐt\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{I}_{t}. Intuitively, this says that the coordinates of d​φt𝒫d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} are almost pairwise independent up to a γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} factor. Note that the ASI factor γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} is proportional to the number of ASI-guarded prefixes in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}, and this dependency is shown to be unavoidable in general [13].

Using standard duality arguments, the feasibility of the SDP (4) was given in [13].

Fact 3.1 (SDP feasibility, [13]).

For any subspace Ht⊆ℝWtH_{t}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} with dim(Ht)≤0.1​|Wt|\dim(H_{t})\leq 0.1|W_{t}| and matrix Et∈ℝ(0.1​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​|Wt|)×WtE_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{(0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}|W_{t}|)\times W_{t}}, the SDP (4) given by constraints (4a)-(4g) is feasible.

In fact, Fact 3.1 is a special case of Theorem A.4 from [13]. For completeness, we include the statement of Theorem A.4 from [13] and explain how it implies Fact 3.1 in Appendix A.
