3.2 Global Interval Tree

As mentioned in Section 3.1, the subspace HtH_{t} in the blocking constraint (4c) and the matrix EtE_{t} in the ASI constraint (4f ASI) are chosen based on the 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure. In this section, we formally describe this data structure and state its properties that we will need.

To simplify our presentation here, we only describe the 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure in the context of choosing the set of γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} many ASI-guarded prefixes ℐt⊆Wt\mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t}, corresponding to the rows of EtE_{t} in the ASI constraint (4f ASI). The choice of the subspace HtH_{t} for the blocking constraint (4c) requires a slight modification of the data structure given here. But as it is only needed for the proof of the ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy in Theorem 1.1, we will defer the details to Section 5.

In Section 3.2.1, we describe how 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} maintains and updates a partition of the complete sliding window [Wt][W_{t}] over time, following the discussion from Section 2.4. Then, in Section 3.2.2 and Section 3.2.3, we prove the properties of 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} that we need.

3.2.1 Interval Representation and Operations

Recall from Section 2.4 that a set of ASI-guarded prefixes ℐt⊆Wt\mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t} can be equivalently viewed as a collection of consecutive intervals that partition the complete sliding window [Wt][W_{t}]. Formally, ℐt={𝒫1,𝒫2,…,𝒫ℓ}\mathcal{I}_{t}=\{\mathcal{P}_{1},\mathcal{P}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{\ell}\} splits [Wt][W_{t}] into consecutive intervals (𝒫j,𝒫j+1](\mathcal{P}_{j},\mathcal{P}_{j+1}], for j=0,⋯,ℓ−1j=0,\cdots,\ell-1 and 𝒫0:=min⁡{Wt}\mathcal{P}_{0}:=\min\{W_{t}\}, along with a final interval (𝒫ℓ,max⁡{Wt}](\mathcal{P}_{\ell},\max\{W_{t}\}] containing all columns in [Wt][W_{t}] larger than 𝒫ℓ\mathcal{P}_{\ell} (see Figure 2). We abuse notation and also use ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} to denote the set of intervals in this partition of [Wt][W_{t}] (we will ignore the final interval (𝒫ℓ,max⁡{Wt}](\mathcal{P}_{\ell},\max\{W_{t}\}]) when the context is clear.

The data structure maintains a set ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} of at most γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} intervals that partitions [Wt][W_{t}] at each step. Recall from Section 2.4 that as the sliding window WtW_{t} progresses, the data structure updates the intervals in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} via two operations: (1) add new intervals to ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} containing newly activated columns in [Wt][W_{t}], or (2) merge consecutive intervals already in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} when their sizes (i.e., number of alive columns contained in them) become too small. We describe these operations formally below.

Initialization and Adding Intervals. Before the process starts, we partition [n][n] into n/sn/s base intervals of size s=20​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨−1​d​log⁡ns=20\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}\,d\log n each, and use ℬ\mathcal{B} to denote this collection of base intervals. At time 00, we initialize ℐ0\mathcal{I}_{0} to be the first |W0|/s=10​d/s|W_{0}|/s=10d/s base intervals contained in W0W_{0}. At each time tt, a base interval I∈ℬI\in\mathcal{B} is called active if I⊆[1,max⁡{Wt}]I\subseteq[1,\max\{W_{t}\}] and I∩Wt≠∅I\cap W_{t}\neq\emptyset (i.e., II contains at least one active column and no column in II is dormant). We add a base interval I∈ℬI\in\mathcal{B} to ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} whenever it becomes active, and we will only add base intervals to ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} throughout.

Remark 3.2.

To ensure that columns in the final interval (𝒫t,max⁡{Wt}](\mathcal{P}_{t},\max\{W_{t}\}] are also controlled by the (4f ASI) constraint, the data structure always includes max⁡{Wt}\max\{W_{t}\} as a “special” ASI-guarded prefix in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}. This ensures that the entire sliding window WtW_{t} also satisfies (4f ASI), and doesn’t affect the SDP feasibility. To simplify our presentation, we will not make this extra ASI constraint explicit.

Merging via a Global Binary Tree.

The intervals in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} are merged

using a global binary tree, denoted by 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, that evolves over time. Initially, 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0} is the complete binary tree of height log⁡(n/s)\log(n/s) whose leaves correspond to all the base intervals ℬ\mathcal{B} (see Figure 5), and at each time tt, tree 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} is a sub-tree of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0}.

Note that the leaves of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0} correspond exactly to the first 10​d/s10d/s base intervals ℐ0\mathcal{I}_{0} when restricted to the sliding window W0W_{0}, and the rest of the leaves to base intervals not yet added to ℐ0\mathcal{I}_{0}. We maintain this property throughout — namely, we ensure that the leaves of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} correspond either to intervals in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}, or to base intervals in ℬ\mathcal{B} that have not been added to ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} yet. We call the former type of leaves of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} active, and refer to them and the intervals in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} interchangeably.

For each active leaf v∈𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾tv\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, we use 𝗌𝗂𝗓𝖾⁡(v)\mathsf{size}(v) to denote the number of alive columns contained in the interval of ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} corresponding to it, and call vv small if 𝗌𝗂𝗓𝖾⁡(v)<s/2\mathsf{size}(v)<s/2. We refer to the two children of each node in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} as left and right child as they appear in Figure 5. A leaf is called a left leaf (resp. right leaf) if it is the left (resp. right) child of its parent. At any time tt, we update 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} by deleting certain active leaves (or equivalently, merging the corresponding interval in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} with one of its neighboring intervals). Formally, our merging rule is the following.1212 12 It may seem natural to use the simple rule of merging two sibling leaves whenever they are both small, but this might create a sequence of Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n) small left leaves (corresponding to a root-leaf path) if the sibling right leaf at the end of this sequence is not yet active. While this sequence of small left leaves is fine for the purpose of maintaining the ASI-guarded prefixes ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}, it will create some technical issues when one tries to adapt the data structure to maintain the subspace HtH_{t} in Section 5. This is why we use the more sophisticated Merging Rule 3.3 instead.

Merging Rule 3.3 (Merging via global binary tree).

At any time tt:

  1. (i)

    For any small left leaf v∈𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾tv\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, delete it and merge its interval with the interval at the next active leaf (see Figure 6 for an illustration); do nothing if vv is the last active leaf.1313 13 The case where an active small left leaf vv is the last active leaf in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} will be ignored throughout our analysis. One can essentially view vv as being deleted and merged with the next base interval when it becomes active. In particular, if the right sibling of vv is also an active leaf, then also delete the right sibling and use their parent to represent the merged interval (see Figure 7).

  2. (ii)

    For any small right leaf v∈𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾tv\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, if the left sibling of vv has been deleted, then delete vv and use its parent to represent its interval (see Figure 8 for an illustratoin).

Intuitively, one can view the merging by Merging Rule 3.3 as happening from left to right — as (i) describes, whenever a left active leaf becomes small, it immediately merges with the active interval on its right if there exists one. The deletion in (ii) is mainly for the purpose of cleaning up 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} when only a single right child of certain nodes in the tree survives.

3.2.2 Bounding the Number of Intervals

Merging Rule 3.3 allows us to lower bound the average size of active leaves in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, and hence to upper bound their number, which is equal to the number of ASI-guarded prefixes |ℐt||\mathcal{I}_{t}|.

Proposition 3.4 (Bounding the number of intervals).

At any time tt, consider 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} after Merging Rule 3.3 is completed. Then the average size of active leaves in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} is at least s/(2​log⁡n)s/(2\log n). Consequently, the total number of active leaves is |ℐt|⩽(2​|Wt|​log⁡n)/s≤γ𝖠𝖲𝖨|\mathcal{I}_{t}|\leqslant(2|W_{t}|\log n)/s\leq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}.

Proof.

Note that there is no small left leaves in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} after Merging Rule 3.3 is completed (except for possibly the last active leaf, which we will ignore as mentioned in Footnote 13), as they all get merged by (i). There might be many small right leaves in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, but we will control their average sizes by charging them to certain non-small active left leaves as follows.

For each small right leaf vv, consider its left sibling ww, which must exist as otherwise vv will be deleted by (ii). Note that in the subtree of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} rooted at ww (which may contain the single node ww if it is an active leaf), there must exist an active non-small left leaf w′w^{\prime}, as otherwise the subtree rooted at ww will get merged by (i). We will charge vv to this non-small left leaf w′w^{\prime}.

Note that each small right leaf that gets charged to w′w^{\prime} is the sibling of one of its ancestors. As w′w^{\prime} can have <log⁡n<\log n ancestors (corresponding to the entire root-leaf path), <log⁡n<\log n small right leaves can be charged to each non-small left leaf w′w^{\prime}. As w′w^{\prime} has size at least s/2s/2, averaging over itself and all the <log⁡n<\log n small right leaves that are charged to it, the average sizes of active leaves in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} is at least s/(2​log⁡n)s/(2\log n). The upper bound on |ℐt||\mathcal{I}_{t}| then follows immediately, as the intervals corresponding to the active leaves of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾t\mathsf{Tree}_{t} form a partition of the sliding window WtW_{t}.

∎

3.2.3 Bounding the Error Sets for Prefixes

Recall from Section 2.4 (also see Section 3.3) that for any 𝒫∈[Wt]\mathcal{P}\in[W_{t}] that is not an ASI-guarded prefix in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}, we call it unguarded, and assign 𝒫t:=max⁡{ℐt∩[𝒫]}\mathcal{P}_{t}:=\max\{\mathcal{I}_{t}\cap[\mathcal{P}]\}, i.e., the maximum-indexed ASI-guarded prefix before 𝒫\mathcal{P}, as its ASI-guard at time tt (see Figure 3). For an ASI-guarded prefix 𝒫∈ℐt\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{I}_{t}, its ASI-guard at time tt is defined to be itself.

Recall that the discrepancy change for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} is decomposed as d​φt𝒫=d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨+d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}, where d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} is the discrepancy change of its ASI-guard 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t}, and d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} is the that of the alive columns between the ASI-guard and 𝒫\mathcal{P}. We refer to this latter set the error columns for 𝒫\mathcal{P} at time tt. The union of error columns for 𝒫\mathcal{P} at all time steps is called its error set, and is formally defined below.

Definition 3.5 (Error set for 𝒫\mathcal{P}).

The error set for 𝒫\mathcal{P} up till time tt, denoted as 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}_{t}, consists of all error columns for 𝒫\mathcal{P} for all time steps t′≤tt^{\prime}\leq t. The error set for 𝒫\mathcal{P} is defined as 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫:=𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋n𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}:=\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}_{n}.

Note that the error set for 𝒫\mathcal{P} depends on the outcomes of the randomness of the algorithm. As discussed in Section 2.4, our bound on φt𝖾𝗋𝗋\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} will depend on how large the error set for 𝒫\mathcal{P} is. Merging Rule 3.3 allows us to give the following upper bound on 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}.

Proposition 3.6 (Bounding the error set).

We always have |𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫|≤(s/2)​log⁡n=O⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨−1​d​log2​n)|\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}|\leq(s/2)\log n=O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}\,d\log^{2}n).

Proof.

Our goal is to find a set |𝒢𝒫|<log⁡n|\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}}|<\log n of nodes in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0} that may contribute to 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}, and show that the subtree rooted at each node in 𝒢𝒫\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}} can contribute at most s/2s/2 to 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}.

To define the node set 𝒢𝒫\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}}, let v𝒫∈ℬv_{\mathcal{P}}\in\mathcal{B} be the leaf of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0} (equivalently, base interval) that contains 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Consider the root-leaf path from the root 𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍0\mathsf{root}_{0} of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0} to v𝒫v_{\mathcal{P}}. Starting from 𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍0\mathsf{root}_{0} and following along this root-leaf path, whenever a node vv on the root-leaf path is the right child of its parent, we add the left sibling of vv to 𝒢𝒫\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}} (see Figure 9 for an illustration).

As the depth of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾0\mathsf{Tree}_{0}, and hence the length of the root-leaf path, is log⁡(n/s)\log(n/s), we have ℓ:=|𝒢𝒫|<(log⁡n)−1\ell:=|\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}}|<(\log n)-1. Denote the nodes in 𝒢𝒫\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{P}} as G𝒫​(1),⋯,G𝒫​(ℓ)G_{\mathcal{P}}(1),\cdots,G_{\mathcal{P}}(\ell). We abuse notation and also use G𝒫​(k)G_{\mathcal{P}}(k) to denote the union of all leaf intervals in the subtree rooted at node G𝒫​(k)G_{\mathcal{P}}(k). Note that the intervals G𝒫​(1),⋯,G𝒫​(ℓ)G_{\mathcal{P}}(1),\cdots,G_{\mathcal{P}}(\ell), together with the (partial) base interval v𝒫∩[𝒫]v_{\mathcal{P}}\cap[\mathcal{P}], form a partition of [𝒫][\mathcal{P}], and these are the only intervals that can contribute to 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}. We bound their contributions below.

For each k∈[ℓ]k\in[\ell], note that as long as the node G𝒫​(k)G_{\mathcal{P}}(k) is not deleted, none of the intervals in its subtree will merge with the interval containing 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and thus contribute no column to 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}. Only when G𝒫​(k)G_{\mathcal{P}}(k) becomes an active (left) leaf that is small can it merge with the interval containing 𝒫\mathcal{P}, but in this case 𝗌𝗂𝗓𝖾⁡(G𝒫​(k))<s/2\mathsf{size}(G_{\mathcal{P}}(k))<s/2 and thus it contributes at most s/2s/2 columns to 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}. As the partial base interval v𝒫∩[𝒫]v_{\mathcal{P}}\cap[\mathcal{P}] can contribute at most 𝗌𝗂𝗓𝖾⁡(v𝒫)≤s\mathsf{size}(v_{\mathcal{P}})\leq s columns to 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}}, the size of 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}} is bounded by (s/2)​ℓ+s≤(s/2)​log⁡n(s/2)\ell+s\leq(s/2)\log n, and this completes the proof.

∎

3.3 A Meta-Analysis

In this subsection, we give a meta-analysis of our algorithms that is common to the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3. The specific instantiations of this meta-analysis and the detailed proofs in these two different settings will be given in the next two sections.

Fix an arbitrary prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n]. Our goal is to obtain a bound on the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of its discrepancy vector φt𝒫\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} (with entries φt𝒫​(i)=⟨Ai𝒫,xt⟩\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)=\langle A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}},x_{t}\rangle) with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), so that we can union bound over all prefixes. Let t∗t^{*} be the first time step when 𝒫∈Wt∗\mathcal{P}\in W_{t^{*}}. As our algorithm ensures that the discrepancy update for the whole sliding window is 00 by SDP constraint (4d), φt∗𝒫=0\varphi_{t^{*}}^{\mathcal{P}}=0 and the discrepancy vector φt𝒫\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}} is entirely due to the coloring update of the alive columns in Wt∗W_{t^{*}} after time t∗t^{*}. In the following, we will condition on Wt∗W_{t^{*}} and analyze the discrepancy update after t∗t^{*}. To keep our notation simple, we drop the superscript 𝒫\mathcal{P} whenever the context is clear.

As mentioned in Section 2.3, we will analyze the dynamics of ‖φt‖22\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2} given by

d​∥φt∥22=∥φt+d​t∥22−∥φt∥22=2​⟨d​φt,φt⟩⏟d​Lt+⟨d​φt,d​φt⟩⏟d​Qt,\displaystyle d\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}=\lVert\varphi_{t+dt}\rVert_{2}^{2}-\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}=2\underbrace{\langle d\varphi_{t},\varphi_{t}\rangle}_{dL_{t}}+\underbrace{\langle d\varphi_{t},d\varphi_{t}\rangle}_{dQ_{t}}, (6)

and bound the processes LtL_{t} and QtQ_{t} (with increments d​LtdL_{t} and d​QtdQ_{t}) separately. It turns out that just using spectral independence (4e SI), [8] already gave a bound on QtQ_{t} that matches Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound for the (more general) ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy setting.

Fact 3.7 (QtQ_{t} bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy, [8]).

Consider the setting of Theorem 1.1. For the algorithm in Section 3.1, one has Qt≤O⁡(d+log⁡n)Q_{t}\leq O(d+\log n) with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n).

The above statement follows from Claim 27 in the proof of Theorem 24 of [8].

Bounding the Linear Term LtL_{t}. The bottleneck for the analysis in [8], which results in their sub-optimal bound, is the linear term LtL_{t}. To apply Freedman’s inequality (see Fact 4.3) for the martingale LtL_{t}, they need to bound its quadratic variation 𝔼t​[(d​Lt)2]\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dL_{t})^{2}], where 𝔼t\mathbb{E}_{t} takes the expectation conditional on the events on before time tt. However, as they have no control over the vector d​φtd\varphi_{t}, they need to apply the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality

𝔼t​[(d​Lt)2]≤𝔼t​[‖d​φt‖22]⋅‖φt‖22.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(dL_{t})^{2}\big]\leq\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|d\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\big]\cdot\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}. (7)

Note that (7) is quite wasteful when d​φtd\varphi_{t} has non-trivial randomness, and our key improvement over [8] comes from the randomness guaranteed by affine spectral independence (4f ASI) for the set of ASI-guarded prefixes in ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t}.

However, as the prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} may not be an ASI-guarded prefix, we don’t have almost pairwise independence for d​φtd\varphi_{t} and thus cannot directly improve over (7). Instead, recall from Section 3.2.3 that we let 𝒫t:=max⁡{ℐt∩[𝒫]}\mathcal{P}_{t}:=\max\{\mathcal{I}_{t}\cap[\mathcal{P}]\} be the ASI-guard for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} at time tt, and decompose d​φtd\varphi_{t} as

d​φt=d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨+d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,\displaystyle d\varphi_{t}=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}, (8)

where d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨:=d​φt𝒫td\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}:=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}_{t}} is the discrepancy change of the ASI-guard 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t}, and d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} is the discrepancy change due to the error columns between 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} and 𝒫\mathcal{P} (see Section 3.2.3). Correspondingly,

d​Lt=⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩+⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩=:d​Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨+d​Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋.\displaystyle dL_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle+\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle=:dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}. (9)

In our analysis, we will control the two terms d​Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and d​Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} separately.

Roughly speaking, the ASI-guard part d​Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} can be bounded better than (7) because d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} always satisfies affine spectral independence (4f ASI), despite that the ASI-guard 𝒫t\mathcal{P}_{t} might change over time. To control the error part d​Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}, note that the 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure guarantees that there will be at most O⁡(s​log⁡n)=O⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨−1​log2​n)O(s\log n)=O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}\log^{2}n) error columns throughout all time steps tt, which allows for a standard Freedman-type analysis. We defer the details of how to bound these two parts of the linear term, depending on the specific problem assumptions, to subsequent sections.

4 ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2} Prefix Discrepancy

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.3, which is restated below for convenience.

See 1.3

We present our algorithm for Theorem 1.3 in Section 4.1 and its analysis in Section 4.2. The proof of Theorem 1.3 will appear in Section 4.2.3.

4.1 Algorithm

Fix γ𝖠𝖲𝖨:=100​d​log⁡n\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}:=100\sqrt{d}\log n and τ:=Θ⁡(d+d3/4​log⁡n+d1/4​log3/2​n)\tau:=\Theta(d+d^{3/4}\log n+d^{1/4}\log^{3/2}n) the target discrepancy bound in Theorem 1.3 (with a large enough constant). The algorithm follows the framework in Section 2.1 and it also uses the 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure as described in Section 3.2 to maintain a set of at most γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} ASI-guarded prefixes ℐt⊆Wt\mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t}.

At each time step tt, the algorithm does the following.

  1. 1.

    If there exists prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n] whose ∥φt𝒫∥2\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{2} exceeds the target τ\tau, it outputs 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT}.

  2. 2.

    Otherwise, it solves the SDP in (4), where Ht=∅H_{t}=\emptyset (i.e., there is no constraint of the form (4c)) and the matrix Et∈ℝd​|ℐt|×WtE_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d|\mathcal{I}_{t}|\times W_{t}} contains a row Ai𝒫​(Wt)A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}(W_{t}) (viewed as a vector in ℝWt\mathbb{R}^{W_{t}} with coordinates 00 in Wt∖[𝒫]W_{t}\setminus[\mathcal{P}]) for every ASI-guarded prefix 𝒫∈ℐt\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{I}_{t} and i∈[d]i\in[d].

By Proposition 3.4 and the setting of s=20​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨−1​d​log⁡ns=20\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log n in Section 3.2.2, the row dimension of EtE_{t} is

d​|ℐt|≤d⋅2​|Wt|​log⁡ns=2​d​|Wt|​log⁡n20​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨−1​d​log⁡n=0.1​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​|Wt|,d|\mathcal{I}_{t}|\leq d\cdot\frac{2|W_{t}|\log n}{s}=\frac{2d|W_{t}|\log n}{20\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log n}=0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}|W_{t}|,

which satisfies the condition of Fact 3.1. Thus the SDP (4) is feasible at every time step tt, and to bound the ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy of this algorithm and prove Theorem 1.3, it suffices to prove that the algorithm does not 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT} with high probability.

4.2 Analysis

Fix any prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n]. We will show that, with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), the ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy ∥φt𝒫∥2\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{2} is at most τ\tau at every time step tt. Since the algorithm runs for 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)\mathsf{poly}(n) steps and there are nn prefixes, a union bound across all time steps and prefixes completes the proof. In the following, we drop the superscript 𝒫\mathcal{P} whenever it is clear from the context.

Road Map for the Analysis. Following the meta-analysis in Section 3.3, at each time step tt, we decompose the change of the squared ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy d​‖φt‖22d\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2} as

d​‖φt‖22=d​Qt+2​(d​Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨+d​Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋).d\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}=dQ_{t}+2(dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}).

Our goal will be to show that for any time t∈[0,n]t\in[0,n], with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),

Qt≤τ2/3,Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨≤τ2/6​ and Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋≤τ2/6.\displaystyle Q_{t}\leq\tau^{2}/3\ ,\quad L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6\ \text{ and }\ \ L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6. (10)

Once the above is shown, then by a union bound, one has ‖φt‖22≤τ2\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\tau^{2} for all time steps tt, which implies that the algorithm doesn’t 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT} with high probability.

For technical reasons, in our analysis, we will use the more stringent stopping condition (than the algorithm 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT}s) based on (10). Namely, if any of the conditions in (10) is violated at any time tt, we will freeze the process xtx_{t} and thus Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨,Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} and QtQ_{t} will have zero increment onward.

Stopping Condition 4.1.

We freeze the process xtx_{t} onward if any of the three conditions in (10), i.e., Qt≤τ2/3Q_{t}\leq\tau^{2}/3, Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨≤τ2/6L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6, and Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋≤τ2/6L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6, is violated.

Note that the modified process given by Stopping Condition 4.1 violates (10) at some time step if and only if the unmodified process xtx_{t} does (at a possibly different time). Because of this equivalence, we will abuse notation and also refer to the modified process as xtx_{t}, and the quadratic and linear terms for the modified process as QtQ_{t}, Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}, and Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}.

For the modified process, we always have

‖φt‖22≤Qt+Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨+Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋≤τ2/3+3​(τ2/6+τ2/6)=τ2.\displaystyle\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}\leq Q_{t}+L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/3+3(\tau^{2}/6+\tau^{2}/6)=\tau^{2}. (11)

We will argue that with probability at most 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/\mathsf{poly}(n), the modified process violates (10), and we will do so by taking a union bound over the probability that each one of the three conditions in (10) gets violated. As discussed in Section 3.3, the bound of Qt≤O⁡(d2+d​log⁡n)≤τ2/3Q_{t}\leq O(d^{2}+d\log n)\leq\tau^{2}/3 with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n) was already shown in [8] (see Fact 3.7).

In Section 4.2.1 and Section 4.2.2 below, we bound Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} in Lemmas 4.2 and 4.4 respectively.

4.2.1 Bounding the ASI-Guard Part Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}

We first bound the ASI-guard term Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} in the following lemma.

Lemma 4.2 (Bounding the ASI-guard part, ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2}).

Consider the algorithm in Section 4.1. For any time tt, with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),

Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨≤τ2/6.L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.

Our proof relies on the following Freedman-type concentration inequality for super-martingales.

Fact 4.3 (Lemma 2.2 in [19]).

Let {Zt:t=0,1,⋯}\{Z_{t}:t=0,1,\cdots\} be a sequence of random variables with increments Δ​Zt:=Zt−Zt−1\Delta Z_{t}:=Z_{t}-Z_{t-1}, such that Z0Z_{0} is deterministic and Δ​Zt≤M\Delta Z_{t}\leq M for all t≥1t\geq 1.

If for all t≥1t\geq 1, we have

𝔼t−1​[Δ​Zt]≤−δ​𝔼t−1​[(Δ​Zt)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\Delta Z_{t}]\leq-\delta\,\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[(\Delta Z_{t})^{2}] (12)

holds with 0<δ<1/M0<\delta<1/M, where 𝔼t−1​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{t-1}[\cdot] denotes 𝔼[⋅|Z1,⋯,Zt−1]\mathbb{E}[\cdot|Z_{1},\cdots,Z_{t-1}]. Then for all ξ≥0\xi\geq 0,

Pr⁡(Zt−Z0>ξ)≤exp⁡(−δ​ξ).\Pr\big(Z_{t}-Z_{0}>\xi\big)\leq\exp(-\delta\xi).
Proof of Lemma 4.2.

Fix a time step t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0, we bound the probability that Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}} exceeds τ2/6\tau^{2}/6.

Recall that φt\varphi_{t} gets its first non-zero increment after the first time t⋆t^{\star} when the sliding window Wt∗W_{t^{*}} contains 𝒫\mathcal{P}. We may assume that t0≥t∗t_{0}\geq t^{*}, as otherwise Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}} will be 00. Following [8], we denote 𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋=𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝒫:=Wt∗∩[𝒫]\mathsf{Corr}=\mathsf{Corr}^{\mathcal{P}}:=W_{t^{*}}\cap[\mathcal{P}] the columns in Wt∗W_{t^{*}} with index at most 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Note that only columns in 𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋\mathsf{Corr} contribute non-zero discrepancy to φt\varphi_{t}. Similar to the analysis in [8, 19, 13], we define the following regularized ASI-guard term

Yt:=Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋xt2​(j),\displaystyle Y_{t}:=L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}x_{t}^{2}(j),

where we set β𝖠𝖲𝖨=Θ⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​log⁡n)\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}=\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log n) for a sufficiently large constant. Below, we will show that the increment d​YtdY_{t} satisfies condition (12) with a suitably chosen factor δ\delta. Here, we naturally map time steps t∈[0,n]t\in[0,n] to {0,1,⋯,n/d​t}\{0,1,\cdots,n/dt\}.

If at any time tt, the modified process xtx_{t} is frozen due to the condition (10) being violated prior to tt, then Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}, and hence YtY_{t}, must have been zero increment at time tt. Thus the increment d​Yt=0dY_{t}=0 trivially satisfies the condition (12) in Fact 4.3 for any δ\delta in this case.

In the other case where the modified process xtx_{t} has not been frozen up till time tt. We will show that condition (12) in Fact 4.3 holds for some factor δ>0\delta>0 by computing the first and second moments of d​YtdY_{t} in the following.

Note that the increment of YtY_{t} is

d​Yt=⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩−2​β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋ut​(j)​xt​(j)​d​t−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋ut​(j)2​d​t.\displaystyle dY_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)^{2}\,dt.

In what follows, all expectations are conditioned on the filtration ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}, or outcome of randomness, up to time tt, and is denoted as 𝔼t[⋅]=𝔼[⋅∣ℱt]\mathbb{E}_{t}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]. Since 𝔼t​[ut]=0\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}]=0, the first moment of d​YtdY_{t} is

𝔼t[dYt]=−β𝖠𝖲𝖨∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t[ut(j)2]dt.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}]=-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt. (13)

The second moment of d​YtdY_{t} is bounded as

𝔼t​[(d​Yt)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dY_{t})^{2}] ≲𝔼t​⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩2+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2⋅𝔼t​(∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋ut​(j)​xt​(j))2​d​t\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\bigr)^{2}dt
≲𝔼t​⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩2+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t​[ut2​(j)]​d​t,\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}\,\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}^{2}(j)]dt,

where we drop lower order terms with scale O⁡((d​t)3/2)O((dt)^{3/2}), use (a+b)2⩽2​a2+2​b2(a+b)^{2}\leqslant 2a^{2}+2b^{2} in the first inequality, and use O⁡(1)O(1)-spectral independence of utu_{t} and that |xt​(j)|≤1|x_{t}(j)|\leq 1 in the second. We bound the first term using affine spectral independence:

𝔼t​⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2} ≤γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑i∈[d]φt​(i)2​𝔼t​[d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨​(i)2]\displaystyle\leq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\sum_{i\in[d]}\varphi_{t}(i)^{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}(i)^{2}\big]
=γ𝖠𝖲𝖨⋅∑i∈[d]φt​(i)2⋅𝔼t​(∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋Ai​(j)​ut​(j))2​d​t≲γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​∥φt∥22​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t​[ut2​(j)]​d​t,\displaystyle=\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot\sum_{i\in[d]}\varphi_{t}(i)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\Big(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)\Big)^{2}dt\lesssim\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}^{2}(j)]dt,

where the first step follows via γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}-affine spectral independence of utu_{t}, and the final step follows by O⁡(1)O(1)-spectral independence of utu_{t} and using |Ai​(j)|≤1|A_{i}(j)|\leq 1 for all i∈[d],j∈[n]i\in[d],j\in[n].

Combining, we get the following bound on the second moment of d​YtdY_{t},

𝔼t​[(d​Yt)2]≲(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​∥φt∥22+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2)​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t​[ut2​(j)]​d​t≤(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​τ2+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2)​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t​[ut2​(j)]​d​t,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dY_{t})^{2}]\lesssim(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}^{2}(j)]\,dt\leq(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\tau^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}^{2}(j)]\,dt, (14)

where we bound ∥φt∥22\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2} by τ2\tau^{2} using (11).

Combining (13) and (14), we get condition (12) with

𝔼t[dYt]≲−(β𝖠𝖲𝖨τ2​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2)⋅𝔼t[(dYt)2].\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}]\lesssim-\Big(\frac{\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\tau^{2}\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}}\Big)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dY_{t})^{2}].

Then applying Freedman-type inequality (Fact 4.3) with deviation ξ=τ2/10\xi=\tau^{2}/10, we obtain

Pr⁡(Yt0−Yt∗≥ξ)≤exp⁡(−ξ​β𝖠𝖲𝖨β𝖠𝖲𝖨2+γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​τ2).\displaystyle\Pr(Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}\geq\xi)\leq\exp\Big(\frac{-\xi\,\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}+\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\tau^{2}}\Big). (15)

To bound the exponent in (15), note that since ξ=τ2/10=Ω⁡(d​log3​n)\xi=\tau^{2}/10=\Omega(\sqrt{d}\log^{3}n) and β𝖠𝖲𝖨=Θ⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​log⁡n)=Θ⁡(d​log2​n)\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}=\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log n)=\Theta(\sqrt{d}\log^{2}n) (as γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=100​d​log⁡n\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=100\sqrt{d}\log n), the first term is bounded as (ξ​β𝖠𝖲𝖨)/β𝖠𝖲𝖨2=Ω⁡(log⁡n)(\xi\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}})/\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}=\Omega(\log n). The second term can be bounded as

ξ​β𝖠𝖲𝖨γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​τ2=(τ2/10)⋅Θ⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​log⁡n)γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​τ2=Θ⁡(log⁡n).\frac{\xi\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\tau^{2}}=\frac{(\tau^{2}/10)\cdot\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log n)}{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\tau^{2}}=\Theta(\log n).

Thus as long as the constant in β𝖠𝖲𝖨\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}} is big enough and the constant in ξ\xi is even (much) larger, the tail probability in (15) is at most 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/\mathsf{poly}(n).

Finally, to compare the target event of Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨≥τ2/6L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 with the event Yt0−Yt∗≥ξY_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}\geq\xi in (15), note that

Yt0−Yt∗\displaystyle Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}} =Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋xt0​(j)2−(0−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋xt∗​(j)2)\displaystyle=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}x_{t_{0}}(j)^{2}-\Big(0-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}x_{t^{*}}(j)^{2}\Big)
=Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋(xt0​(j)2−xt∗​(j)2)≥Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​(10​d)≥Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨−τ2/15,\displaystyle=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}(x_{t_{0}}(j)^{2}-x_{t^{*}}(j)^{2})\ \geq\ L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}(10d)\ \geq\ L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\tau^{2}/15,

where we used that β𝖠𝖲𝖨​d=Θ⁡(d3/2​log2​n)\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}d=\Theta(d^{3/2}\log^{2}n) and τ2=Ω⁡(d3/2​log2​n)\tau^{2}=\Omega(d^{3/2}\log^{2}n) (with a much larger constant). Consequently, the event Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨≥τ2/6L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 implies that Yt0−Yt∗≥τ2/10Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}\geq\tau^{2}/10, and thus,

Pr⁡(Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨≥τ2/6)≤Pr⁡(Yt0−Yt∗≥ξ)≤1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n).\Pr\big(L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6\big)\leq\Pr(Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{*}}\geq\xi)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n).

Taking a union bound over all time steps t0t_{0} completes the proof of the lemma.

∎

4.2.2 Bounding the Error Part Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}

Next, we show how to bound the error term Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} in the following lemma.

Lemma 4.4 (Bounding the error part, ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ2\ell_{2}).

Consider the algorithm in Section 4.1. With probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), we have

Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋≤τ2/6.L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.
Proof of Lemma 4.4.

Fix t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0, we bound the probability that Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}} exceeds τ2/6\tau^{2}/6. Again we may assume that t0≥t∗t_{0}\geq t^{*}, where t∗t^{*} is the time step when prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} first enters the time window.

Recall from Section 3.2 that 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}} (resp. 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝒫\mathsf{Error}_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}) is the set of columns that contribute to the error term Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} throughout the algorithm (resp. up till time tt). The set 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t\mathsf{Error}_{t}, as a (random) function of tt, is monotonically non-decreasing with several “jumps”, corresponding to the times when the interval containing 𝒫\mathcal{P} merges in the 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure.

We drop the superscript 𝒫\mathcal{P} below.

We define the following regularized process for Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},

Zt:=Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋−β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋txt​(j)2,\displaystyle Z_{t}:=L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}x_{t}(j)^{2},

where β𝖾𝗋𝗋:=Θ⁡(d​log⁡n)\beta_{\mathsf{err}}:=\Theta(d\log n) for a large enough constant. Note that whenever 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t\mathsf{Error}_{t} has a “jump”, ZtZ_{t} decreases which is only helpful for us (and thus can be safely ignored henceforth).

Similar to the proof of Lemma 4.2, the condition (12) is trivially satisfied if the modified process was frozen prior to time tt. If the process was not frozen, the increment of ZtZ_{t} is given by

d​Zt=⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩−2​β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tut​(j)​xt​(j)​d​t−β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tut​(j)2​d​t.\displaystyle dZ_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)^{2}dt.

Since both d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} and utu_{t} are mean-zero, the first moment of d​ZtdZ_{t} is:

𝔼t[dZt]=−β𝖾𝗋𝗋∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝔼t[ut(j)2]dt.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}]=-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\,\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt. (16)

The second moment can be bounded as

𝔼t​[(d​Zt)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(dZ_{t})^{2}\big] =𝔼t​(⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩−2​β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tut​(j)​xt​(j)​d​t)2\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\Big(\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}\Big)^{2}
≲𝔼t​[⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩2]+β𝖾𝗋𝗋2⋅𝔼t​(∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tut​(j)​xt​(j))2​d​t\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}\big]+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\Big(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\Big)^{2}dt
≲𝔼t​[‖d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋‖22]⋅‖φt‖22+β𝖾𝗋𝗋2⋅∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝔼⁡[ut​(j)2]​d​t,\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\|_{2}^{2}\big]\cdot\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\cdot\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt,

where in the last inequality, we apply Cauchy-Schwartz inequality for the first term, and for the second term, we use that the vector utu_{t} is O⁡(1)O(1)-spectrally independent and that each |xt​(j)|≤1|x_{t}(j)|\leq 1. To bound 𝔼t​[‖d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋‖22]\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\|_{2}^{2}\bigr] in the first term, we note that d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋​(i)=∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tAi​(j)​ut​(j)​d​td\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}(i)=\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}. Then using that utu_{t} is O⁡(1)O(1)-spectrally independent and each |Ai​(j)|≤1|A_{i}(j)|\leq 1, we can bound

𝔼t​[‖d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋‖22]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[\|d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\|_{2}^{2}\big] =∑i∈[d]𝔼t​[(d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋​(i))2]≲∑i∈[d]∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tAi​(j)2⋅𝔼t​[ut​(j)2]​d​t≤d​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝔼t​[ut​(j)2]​d​t.\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}(i))^{2}\big]\lesssim\sum_{i\in[d]}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}A_{i}(j)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt\leq d\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\,\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt.

Plugging this into the above gives the bound

𝔼t​[(d​Zt)2]≤(d​‖φt‖22+β𝖾𝗋𝗋2)⋅∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝔼t​[ut​(j)2]​d​t.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(dZ_{t})^{2}\big]\leq\big(d\|\varphi_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\big)\cdot\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt. (17)

Combining (16) and (17) gives us condition (12) with

𝔼t[dZt]≤−(β𝖾𝗋𝗋τ2​d+β𝖾𝗋𝗋2)⋅𝔼t[(dZt)2].\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}]\leq-\Big(\frac{\beta_{\mathsf{err}}}{\tau^{2}d+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}}\Big)\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dZ_{t})^{2}].

Applying Freedman-type inequality (Fact 4.3) for deviation ξ=τ2/10\xi=\tau^{2}/10, we get

Pr⁡(Zt0−Zt∗≥ξ)≤exp⁡(−β𝖾𝗋𝗋​ξβ𝖾𝗋𝗋2+τ2​d)≤1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n),\displaystyle\Pr(Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{*}}\geq\xi)\leq\exp\Big(\frac{-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\,\xi}{\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}+\tau^{2}d}\Big)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n), (18)

where the last inequality is obtained by using β𝖾𝗋𝗋=Θ⁡(d​log⁡n)\beta_{\mathsf{err}}=\Theta(d\log n) (and thus (β𝖾𝗋𝗋​ξ)/(τ2​d)=Ω⁡(log⁡n)(\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\xi)/(\tau^{2}d)=\Omega(\log n)), and that ξ=τ2/10=Ω⁡(d3/2​log2​n)\xi=\tau^{2}/10=\Omega(d^{3/2}\log^{2}n) (which implies that (β𝖾𝗋𝗋​ξ)/β𝖾𝗋𝗋2=Ω⁡(d1/2​log⁡n)(\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\xi)/\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}=\Omega(d^{1/2}\log n)).

Finally, we note that the event Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋≥τ2/6L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 implies the event Zt0−Zt∗≥τ2/10Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{*}}\geq\tau^{2}/10, because

Zt0−Zt∗\displaystyle Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{*}} =Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋−β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t0(xt0​(j)2−xt∗​(j)2)≥Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋−β𝖾𝗋𝗋⋅|𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋|\displaystyle=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t_{0}}}\big(x_{t_{0}}(j)^{2}-x_{t^{*}}(j)^{2}\big)\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\cdot|\mathsf{Error}|
≥Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋−β𝖾𝗋𝗋⋅O⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨−1​d​log2​n)=Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋−O⁡(1)⋅d2​log3​nd​log⁡n≥Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋−τ2/15,\displaystyle\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\cdot O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log^{2}n)=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-O(1)\cdot\frac{d^{2}\log^{3}n}{\sqrt{d}\log n}\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\tau^{2}/15,

where the first inequality in the second line uses the error set bound of |𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋|≤O⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨−1​d​log2​n)|\mathsf{Error}|\leq O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log^{2}n) in Proposition 3.6, the equality there uses our parameter setting β𝖾𝗋𝗋=Θ⁡(d​log⁡n)\beta_{\mathsf{err}}=\Theta(d\log n) and γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=100​d​log⁡n\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=100\sqrt{d}\log n, and the final inequality uses τ2=Ω⁡(d3/2​log2​n)\tau^{2}=\Omega(d^{3/2}\log^{2}n) (with a large enough constant).

Combining everything, we get Pr⁡(Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋≥τ2/6)≤1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)\Pr(L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}\geq\tau^{2}/6)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n) and this completes the proof. ∎

4.2.3 Putting Things Together

Now we are ready to put things together and prove Theorem 1.3.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

We run the algorithm in Section 4.1, and we have already shown there that the SDP is always feasible. Combining Fact 3.7, Lemma 4.2 and Lemma 4.4, the probability that any of the three (modified) processes Qt,Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨Q_{t},L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} violates Stopping Condition 4.1 and (10) is at most 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/\mathsf{poly}(n). As this stopping condition implies the target discrepancy bound ‖φt𝒫‖2≤τ\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{2}\leq\tau, by taking a union bound over all time steps and prefixes 𝒫\mathcal{P}, the algorithm never outputs 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT} with probability at least 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n). Finally, rounding the coloring of each dead column to ±1\pm 1 incurs at most O⁡(1)O(1) additive ℓ2\ell_{2} discrepancy. This proves the theorem. ∎

5 ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} Prefix Discrepancy

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.1, which is restated below.

See 1.1

We give our algorithm for Theorem 1.1 in Section 5.1 and its analysis in Section 5.2. The proof of Theorem 1.1 will appear in Section 5.2.3. For our analysis, we also need to use an ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} bound on the prefix discrepancy ∥φt𝒫∥∞\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{\infty} for every prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n], which will be given in Section 5.3.

5.1 Algorithm

Fix γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=100d(logn)−1/2\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=100\sqrt{d}\,(\log n)^{-1/2}, and let τ:=Θ⁡(d+d1/4​log7/4​n)\tau:=\Theta(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\log^{7/4}n) be the target discrepancy bound in Theorem 1.1 (with a large enough constant). Also set λ:=Θ⁡(log3/2⁡n)\lambda:=\Theta(\log^{3/2}n) to be our target ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound (see Lemma 5.2). Analogous to Algorithm 4.1, our algorithm here follows the framework in Sections 2.1 and 3.1, where it uses the 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure from Section 3.2 to maintain a set of at most γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}} ASI-guarded prefixes ℐt⊆Wt\mathcal{I}_{t}\subseteq W_{t}.

The main difference from Section 4.1 is that our algorithm also uses a slightly modified version of 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}, denoted as 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty}, to choose a subspace HtH_{t} to enforce the blocking constraints (4d). This is only for controlling the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy, and we defer its detail to Section 5.3.

Formally, at each time step tt, the algorithm does the following.

  1. 1.

    If there exists 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n], for which either ∥φt𝒫∥2\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{2} exceeds the target ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy bound τ\tau, or ∥φt𝒫∥∞\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{\infty} exceeds the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound λ\lambda, it outputs 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT}.

  2. 2.

    Otherwise, it solves the SDP in (4), where HtH_{t} is the subspace output by 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} and the matrix Et∈ℝd​|ℐt|×WtE_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d|\mathcal{I}_{t}|\times W_{t}} contains a row Ai𝒫​(Wt)A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}}(W_{t}) for every ASI-guarded prefix 𝒫∈ℐt\mathcal{P}\in\mathcal{I}_{t} and i∈[d]i\in[d].

Analogous to Algorithm 4.1, the row dimension of EtE_{t} is at most 0.1​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​|Wt|0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}|W_{t}| (as we use the same parameters in 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}). By Proposition 5.8, the dimension of HtH_{t} is at most 0.1​|Wt|0.1|W_{t}|. This satisfies the conditions of Fact 3.1 and hence SDP (3.1) is always feasible. In the remainder, we show that the algorithm does not 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT} with high probability.

5.2 Analysis

Fix any prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n]. We will show that, with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), the ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy is bounded as ∥φt𝒫∥2≤τ\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{2}\leq\tau and the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy is bounded as ∥φt𝒫∥∞≤λ\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda at any time step tt. Since the algorithm runs for 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)\mathsf{poly}(n) steps and there are nn prefixes, a union bound across all time steps and prefixes completes the proof. In the following, we drop the superscript 𝒫\mathcal{P} whenever it is clear from the context.

Road Map for the Analysis. Following the meta-analysis in Section 3.3 and the analysis in Section 4.2, we decompose the change of ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy d​∥φt∥22d\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2} as,

d​∥φt∥22=d​Qt+2​(d​Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨+d​Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋).d\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}=dQ_{t}+2(dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}+dL_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}).

Our goal will be to show for any time t∈[0,n]t\in[0,n], with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),

Qt≤τ2/3,Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨≤τ2/6,Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋≤τ2/6​ and ∥φt∥∞≤λ,\displaystyle Q_{t}\leq\tau^{2}/3\ ,\quad L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6\ ,\quad L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6\ \text{ and }\ \ \lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda, (19)

where the extra condition ∥φt∥∞≤λ\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda is needed for controlling the ASI-guard part Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}.

Once the above is shown, then by a union bound, one has ∥φt∥22≤τ2\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\tau^{2} and ∥φt∥∞≤λ\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda for all time steps tt, which implies that the algorithm doesn’t 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT} with high probability. Analogous to Section 5.2, we use the following stopping condition for our analysis.

Stopping Condition 5.1.

We freeze xtx_{t} onward if any of the four conditions in (19), i.e. Qt≤τ2/3Q_{t}\leq\tau^{2}/3, Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨≤τ2/6L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6, Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋≤τ2/6L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6, and ∥φt∥∞≤λ\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}\leq\lambda is violated.

The bound for Qt≤O⁡(d+log⁡n)≤τ2/3Q_{t}\leq O(d+\log n)\leq\tau^{2}/3 with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n) was already shown in [8] (see Fact 3.7). In Section 5.2.1 and Section 5.2.2, we bound Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} in Lemmas 5.3 and Lemma 5.4 respectively. Finally, in Section 5.3, we will describe the modified data structure 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} that allows us to obtain the following bound on ∥φt∥∞\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}.1414 14 We remark that in the current setting, there are algorithms (e.g., [2]) that achieve the better ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound of O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n). However, these algorithms and analysis are quite different from ours, and it is unclear how to achieve the same improvement for the framework that we use here.

Lemma 5.2 (ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound).

Consider the algorithm in Section 5.1 and the data structure in Section 5.3. For any time tt, and every prefix 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n], with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),

∥φt𝒫∥∞≤O⁡(log3/2⁡n).\lVert\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\rVert_{\infty}\leq O(\log^{3/2}n).

5.2.1 Bounding the ASI-Guard Part Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}

We first show a bound on the 𝖠𝖲𝖨\mathsf{ASI}-guard term Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} in the following lemma.

Lemma 5.3 (Bounding the ASI-guard part, ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2}).

Consider the algorithm in Section 5.1. For any time tt, with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n),

Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨≤τ2/6.L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.

Our proof follows the same strategy as Lemmas 4.2 and 4.4, where we apply Freedman-type concentration for super-martingales.

Proof.

For a time step t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0, we bound the probability that Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}} exceeds τ2/6\tau^{2}/6.

We let 𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋=𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝒫:=Wt⋆∩𝒫\mathsf{Corr}=\mathsf{Corr}^{\mathcal{P}}:=W_{t^{\star}}\cap\mathcal{P} be the set of columns in Wt⋆W_{t^{\star}} with index at most 𝒫\mathcal{P}, where t⋆t^{\star} is the first time the window Wt⋆W_{t^{\star}} contains 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Recall from the proof of Lemma 4.2 that φt\varphi_{t} incurs a non-zero discrepancy only on columns in 𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋\mathsf{Corr}. We define the corresponding regularized ASI-guard term as,

Yt:=Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋xt​(j)2,Y_{t}:=L_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}x_{t}(j)^{2},

where we set β𝖠𝖲𝖨=O⁡(1)\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}=O(1) for a sufficiently large constant. Below, we show that d​YtdY_{t} satisfies the conditions of Freedman-type concentration (Fact 4.3) for a suitably chosen δ\delta. Like before, we map time steps t∈[0,n]t\in[0,n] to {0,1,…​n/d​t}\{0,1,\ldots n/dt\}.

For time steps tt, where xtx_{t} is frozen due to (19) being violated prior to tt, then d​Lt𝖠𝖲𝖨dL_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}} and d​YtdY_{t} equal 00 and trivially satisfy (12) in Fact 4.3 for any δ\delta. In the other case, we show that condition 12 in Fact 4.3 holds for an appropriate δ>0\delta>0, by computing the first and the second moment of d​YtdY_{t}. The increment of YtY_{t} is,

d​Yt=⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩−2​β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋ut​(j)​xt​(j)​d​t−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋ut​(j)2​d​t.dY_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\,\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)^{2}dt.

Conditioning on the filtration ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} (or equivalently the outcome of randomness up to time tt), the first moment of d​YtdY_{t} is

𝔼t[dYt]=−β𝖠𝖲𝖨∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t[ut(j)2].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}]=-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]. (20)

The second moment of d​YtdY_{t} is bounded as,

𝔼t​[d​Yt2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}^{2}] ≲𝔼t​⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩2+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2⋅𝔼t​(∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋ut​(j)​xt​(j))2​d​t\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\bigr)^{2}dt
≲𝔼t​⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩2+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t​[ut​(j)2]​d​t,\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt,

where we drop lower order terms with scale O⁡((d​t)3/2)O((dt)^{3/2}), use (a+b)2≤2​a2+2​b2(a+b)^{2}\leq 2a^{2}+2b^{2} in the first inequality, and use O⁡(1)O(1)-spectral independence of utu_{t} and that |xt​(j)|≤1|x_{t}(j)|\leq 1 in the second inequality. We bound the first term using affine spectral independence.

𝔼t​⟨d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨,φt⟩2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2} ≤γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​∑i∈[d]φt​(i)2⋅𝔼t​[d​φt𝖠𝖲𝖨​(i)2]\displaystyle\leq\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\sum_{i\in[d]}\varphi_{t}(i)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{ASI}}(i)^{2}\bigr]
=γ𝖠𝖲𝖨⋅∑i∈[d]φt​(i)2⋅𝔼t​(∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋Ai​(j)​ut​(j))2≲γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​∥φt∥∞2​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t​[ut​(j)2]​d​t,\displaystyle=\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot\sum_{i\in[d]}\varphi_{t}(i)^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}A_{i}(j)u_{t}(j)\bigr)^{2}\lesssim\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt,

where the first step uses γ𝖠𝖲𝖨\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}-affine spectral independence of utu_{t}, and the final step uses that utu_{t} is O⁡(1)O(1)-spectral independence, ∑i∈[d]Ai​(j)2≤1\sum_{i\in[d]}A_{i}(j)^{2}\leq 1 for all j∈[n]j\in[n] and the ℓ1\ell_{1}-ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} Hölder’s inequality.

Combining, we get the following bound on the second moment of d​YtdY_{t},

𝔼t​[d​Yt2]≲(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​∥φt∥∞2+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2)​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t​[ut​(j)2]​d​t≤(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​λ2+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2)​∑j∈𝖢𝗈𝗋𝗋𝔼t​[ut​(j)2]​d​t,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}^{2}]\lesssim(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt\leq(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lambda^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Corr}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]dt, (21)

where we bound ∥φt∥∞2≤λ2\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{\infty}^{2}\leq\lambda^{2} by Lemma 5.2. Combining (20) and (21), we get condition (12) with,

𝔼t​[d​Yt]≲−(β𝖠𝖲𝖨λ2​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨+β𝖠𝖲𝖨2)​𝔼t​[d​Yt2].\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}]\lesssim-\bigl(\frac{\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\lambda^{2}\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}+\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}}\bigr)\mathbb{E}_{t}[dY_{t}^{2}].

Then applying Freedman-type inequality (Fact 4.3), with deviation ξ=Θ⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​log4​n)\xi=\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log^{4}n), we obtain

Pr⁡(Yt−Yt⋆≥ξ)≤exp⁡(−ξ​β𝖠𝖲𝖨β𝖠𝖲𝖨2+γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​λ2).\displaystyle\Pr(Y_{t}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq\xi)\leq\exp(\frac{-\xi\,\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}+\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lambda^{2}}). (22)

To bound the exponent in (22), note that since ξ=Θ⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​log4​n)=Θ⁡(d​log3.5​n)\xi=\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log^{4}n)=\Theta(\sqrt{d}\log^{3.5}n) and β𝖠𝖲𝖨=O⁡(1)\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}=O(1) (for sufficiently large constants), the first term is bounded as (ξ​β𝖠𝖲𝖨)/β𝖠𝖲𝖨2=Ω⁡(log⁡n)(\xi\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}})/\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{2}=\Omega(\log n). The second term can be bounded as,

ξ​β𝖠𝖲𝖨γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​λ2=Θ⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨​log4​n)γ𝖠𝖲𝖨⋅O⁡(log3⁡n)=Θ⁡(log⁡n).\frac{\xi\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}}{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\lambda^{2}}=\frac{\Theta(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\log^{4}n)}{\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}\cdot O(\log^{3}n)}=\Theta(\log n).

Note that as before,

Yt0−Yt⋆≥Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨−β𝖠𝖲𝖨​(10​d).Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}-\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}(10d).

As τ2=Θ⁡(d+d​log3.5​n)\tau^{2}=\Theta(d+\sqrt{d}\log^{3.5}n) (with a much larger constant), τ2/6≥β𝖠𝖲𝖨​(10​d)+ξ\tau^{2}/6\geq\beta_{\mathsf{ASI}}(10d)+\xi. Consequently, the event Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨≥τ2/6L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 implies that Yt0−Yt⋆≥ξY_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq\xi and thus,

Pr⁡(Lt0𝖠𝖲𝖨≥τ2/6)≤Pr⁡(Yt0−Yt⋆≥ξ)≤1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n).\Pr(L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{ASI}}\geq\tau^{2}/6)\leq\Pr(Y_{t_{0}}-Y_{t^{\star}}\geq\xi)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n).

5.2.2 Bounding the Error Part Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}

Next, we bound the error term Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} in the following lemma.

Lemma 5.4 (Bounding the error part, ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2}).

Consider the algorithm in Section 5.1. With probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), we have

Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋≤τ2/6.L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}\leq\tau^{2}/6.
Proof.

For t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0, we bound the probability that Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}} exceeds τ2/6\tau^{2}/6.

Analogous to the proof of Lemma 4.4, we define the sets 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋𝒫\mathsf{Error}^{\mathcal{P}} (which we denote by 𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋\mathsf{Error} for shorthand). The regularized process for Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}:

Zt=Lt𝖾𝗋𝗋−β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝒫xt​(j)2,\displaystyle Z_{t}=L_{t}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}}x_{t}(j)^{2}, (23)

where β𝖾𝗋𝗋=O⁡(log⁡n)\beta_{\mathsf{err}}=O(\log n). Analogous to the proofs of Lemma 4.2, Lemma 4.4 and Lemma 5.3, we analyze the increments at a time tt before the process has frozen. The increment of d​ZtdZ_{t} is given by,

d​Zt=⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩−2​β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tut​(j)​xt​(j)​d​t−β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tut​(j)2.\displaystyle dZ_{t}=\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)^{2}. (24)

Since d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}} and utu_{t} are mean-zero, the first moment of d​ZtdZ_{t} is:

𝔼t[dZt]=−β𝖾𝗋𝗋∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝔼t[ut(j)2].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}]=-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{t}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]. (25)

The second moment can be bounded as,

𝔼t​[(d​Zt)2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[(dZ_{t})^{2}] =𝔼t​(⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩−2​β𝖾𝗋𝗋​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tut​(j)​xt​(j)​d​t)2\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle-2\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\sqrt{dt}\bigr)^{2}
≲𝔼t​[⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩2]+β𝖾𝗋𝗋2⋅𝔼t​(∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋tut​(j)​xt​(j))2​d​t\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}]+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}u_{t}(j)x_{t}(j)\bigr)^{2}dt
≲𝔼t​[⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩2]+β𝖾𝗋𝗋2​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t𝔼⁡[ut​(j)2],\displaystyle\lesssim\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}]+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}],

where we ignore the terms of scale O⁡(d​t3/2)O(dt^{3/2}) as they are lower order and the second inequality follows via O⁡(1)O(1)-spectral independence of utu_{t}. We bound the first term as follows:

𝔼t​[⟨d​φt𝖾𝗋𝗋,φt⟩2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[\langle d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{err}},\varphi_{t}\rangle^{2}] =𝔼t​(∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t∩𝒱tut​(j)​((Wt𝒫)⊤​φt)​(j))2\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl(\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}u_{t}(j)((W_{t}^{\mathcal{P}})^{\top}\varphi_{t})(j)\bigr)^{2}
≲∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t∩𝒱t𝔼t​[ut​(j)2​((Wt𝒫)⊤​φt)​(j)2]≤∥φt∥22​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t∩𝒱t𝔼⁡[ut​(j)2].\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[u_{t}(j)^{2}((W_{t}^{\mathcal{P}})^{\top}\varphi_{t})(j)^{2}\bigr]\leq\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}].

Combining we get,

𝔼t​[d​Zt2]≲(∥φt∥22+β𝖾𝗋𝗋2)​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t∩𝒱t𝔼⁡[ut​(j)2]≲(τ2+β𝖾𝗋𝗋2)​∑j∈𝖤𝗋𝗋𝗈𝗋t∩𝒱t𝔼⁡[ut​(j)2],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}^{2}]\lesssim(\lVert\varphi_{t}\rVert_{2}^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}]\ \lesssim(\tau^{2}+\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2})\sum_{j\in\mathsf{Error}_{t}\cap\mathcal{V}_{t}}\mathbb{E}[u_{t}(j)^{2}], (26)

where the second inequality follows as the process has not frozen yet. This satisfies the Condition (12) in Fact 4.3 as,

𝔼t​[d​Zt]≲(−β𝖾𝗋𝗋​ξβ𝖾𝗋𝗋2+τ2)​𝔼t​[d​Zt2].\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}]\lesssim\bigl(\frac{-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\,\xi}{\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}+\tau^{2}}\bigr)\mathbb{E}_{t}[dZ_{t}^{2}].

Applying Freedman-type inequality for deviation ξ=τ2/10\xi=\tau^{2}/10, we get

Pr⁡(Zt−Z0≥ξ)≤exp⁡(−ξ​β𝖾𝗋𝗋β𝖾𝗋𝗋2+τ2)=1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(𝗇),\Pr(Z_{t}-Z_{0}\geq\xi)\leq\exp(\frac{-\xi\,\beta_{\mathsf{err}}}{\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}+\tau^{2}})=1/\mathsf{poly(n)},

where the last inequality is obtained by using that β𝖾𝗋𝗋=O⁡(log⁡n)\beta_{\mathsf{err}}=O(\log n) and ξ=τ2/10\xi=\tau^{2}/10, where τ2=O⁡(d+d​log7/2​n)\tau^{2}=O(d+\sqrt{d}\log^{7/2}n). This implies that (ξ​β𝖾𝗋𝗋)/β𝖾𝗋𝗋2=Ω⁡(d1/2​log7/2​n/log⁡n)(\xi\beta_{\mathsf{err}})/\beta_{\mathsf{err}}^{2}=\Omega(d^{1/2}\log^{7/2}n/\log n) which is Ω⁡(log⁡n)\Omega(\log n) and (ξ​β𝖾𝗋𝗋/τ2)=β𝖾𝗋𝗋/10=Ω⁡(log⁡n)(\xi\beta_{\mathsf{err}}/\tau^{2})=\beta_{\mathsf{err}}/10=\Omega(\log n) provided the constant in β𝖾𝗋𝗋\beta_{\mathsf{err}} is large enough.

Finally, similar to the proof of Lemma 4.4, the event Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋≥τ2/6L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}\geq\tau^{2}/6 implies the event Zt0−Zt⋆≥τ2/10Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{\star}}\geq\tau^{2}/10. In particular, using τ2=Θ⁡(d+d1/2​log7/2​n)\tau^{2}=\Theta(d+d^{1/2}\log^{7/2}n) for a large enough constant, we have

Zt0−Zt⋆≥Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋−β𝖾𝗋𝗋⋅O⁡(γ𝖠𝖲𝖨−1​d​log2​n)=Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋−O⁡(1)⋅d​log3​nd(logn)−1/2≥Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋−τ2/10.Z_{t_{0}}-Z_{t^{\star}}\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\beta_{\mathsf{err}}\cdot O(\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}^{-1}d\log^{2}n)=L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-O(1)\cdot\frac{d\log^{3}n}{\sqrt{d}(\log n)^{-1/2}}\geq L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}-\tau^{2}/10.

Combining everything, we get Pr⁡(Lt0𝖾𝗋𝗋≥τ2/6)≤1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)\Pr(L_{t_{0}}^{\mathsf{err}}\geq\tau^{2}/6)\leq 1/\mathsf{poly}(n), and this completes the proof. ∎

5.2.3 Putting Things Together

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Consider the algorithm in Section 5.1. There, we have already shown that the SDP at each step of the algorithm is feasible. Combining Fact 3.7, Lemma 5.2, Lemma 5.3 and Lemma 5.4, the probability that any of the four conditions in (19) is violated is at most 1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1/\mathsf{poly}(n). by taking a union bound over all time steps and prefixes 𝒫\mathcal{P}, the algorithm never outputs 𝖠𝖡𝖮𝖱𝖳\mathsf{ABORT} with probability at least 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n). Finally, rounding the coloring of each dead column to ±1\pm 1 incurs at most O⁡(1)O(1) additive ℓ2\ell_{2} discrepancy, and this completes the proof. ∎

5.3 Bounding ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} Prefix Discrepancy

In this section, we describe the data structure 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} and prove Lemma 5.2, restated below.

See 5.2

To bound the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy, we will enforce a set of blocking constraints (corresponding to HtH_{t} in (4c)). We describe these constraints and how it controls ‖φt𝒫‖∞\|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}\|_{\infty} in Section 5.3.1. Then in Section 5.3.2, we present the modified data structure 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} for maintaining these blocking constraints and analyze its properties. Finally, we prove Lemma 5.2 in Section 5.3.3.

5.3.1 Our Strategy

We follow the approach in [8] of bounding the prefix discrepancy |φt𝒫​(i)||\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)| for each row i∈[d]i\in[d]. Recall that φt𝒫​(i)\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i) only incurs non-zero discrepancy when 𝒫∈Wt\mathcal{P}\in W_{t} (due to constraint (4d)). To control its discrepancy while 𝒫∈Wt\mathcal{P}\in W_{t}, we impose a set of blocking constraints (i.e., Ht≠∅H_{t}\neq\emptyset in (4c)). We fix an arbitrary row i∈[d]i\in[d] and describe the blocking constraints for row ii below.

At each time step tt, we maintain a subset 𝒥i,t⊆Wt\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\subseteq W_{t} and include the prefix Ai𝒫′A_{i}^{\mathcal{P}^{\prime}} of row ii into the subspace HtH_{t} for each 𝒫′∈𝒥i,t\mathcal{P}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{J}_{i,t}, i.e., we ensure that d​φt𝒫′​(i)=0d\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P^{\prime}}}(i)=0 for any 𝒫′∈𝒥i,t\mathcal{P}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{J}_{i,t}. We require ∑i∈[d]|𝒥i,t|≤0.1​|Wt|\sum_{i\in[d]}|\mathcal{J}_{i,t}|\leq 0.1|W_{t}| to ensure that dim(Ht)≤0.1​|Wt|\dim(H_{t})\leq 0.1|W_{t}|, as needed in Fact 3.1. The data structure 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} that maintains the sets {𝒥i,t}i∈[d]\{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\}_{i\in[d]} will be given in Section 5.3.2. Here, we show to bound |φt𝒫​(i)||\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)|, and we drop the superscript 𝒫\mathcal{P} below when the context is clear.

Bad Columns for 𝒫\mathcal{P}, and Bounding |φt​(i)||\varphi_{t}(i)|. Borrowing terminology from Section 3.2, we call 𝒥i,t\mathcal{J}_{i,t} the blocking-guarded prefixes for row ii, and call the remaining prefixes unguarded for row ii. For each unguarded prefix 𝒫∈[Wt]\mathcal{P}\in[W_{t}] for row ii, we call max⁡{𝒥i,t∩[𝒫]}\max\{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\cap[\mathcal{P}]\}, i.e., the maximum-indexed blocking-guarded prefix prior to 𝒫\mathcal{P}, its blocking-guard for row ii. The alive columns between the blocking-guard and 𝒫\mathcal{P} will be called bad columns. Analogous to Definition 3.5, we define the following notation of bad set for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} in row ii.

Definition 5.5 (Bad set for 𝒫\mathcal{P} in row ii).

The bad set for prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} in row ii up to time tt, denoted as 𝖡𝖺𝖽i,t𝒫\mathsf{Bad}_{i,t}^{\mathcal{P}}, is the union of all bad columns for 𝒫\mathcal{P} at all time steps t′≤tt^{\prime}\leq t. The bad set for 𝒫\mathcal{P} is defined as 𝖡𝖺𝖽i𝒫:=𝖡𝖺𝖽i,n𝒫\mathsf{Bad}^{\mathcal{P}}_{i}:=\mathsf{Bad}^{\mathcal{P}}_{i,n}.

Note that the blocking-guard of prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} incurs zero discrepancy change at time tt, and thus

d​φt​(i)=d​φt𝖻𝖺𝖽​(i),d\varphi_{t}(i)=d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{bad}}(i),

where d​φt𝖻𝖺𝖽​(i)d\varphi_{t}^{\mathsf{bad}}(i) is the discrepancy change due to the bad columns for row ii at time tt (see Figure 10).

It turns out that the contribution of the bad columns depends on their ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass, where we define the ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass of a set S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n] in row ii to be ‖Ai​(S)‖22=∑j∈SAi​(j)2\|A_{i}(S)\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{j\in S}A_{i}(j)^{2}. In particular, [8, Theorem 1] gives the bound |φt​(i)|≤O⁡(‖Ai​(𝖡𝖺𝖽i)‖22⋅log⁡n)|\varphi_{t}(i)|\leq O(\sqrt{\|A_{i}(\mathsf{Bad}_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\log n}) with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n).

Therefore, to obtain the result in Lemma 5.2, we need to bound ‖Ai​(𝖡𝖺𝖽i)‖22≤O⁡(log2⁡n)\|A_{i}(\mathsf{Bad}_{i})\|_{2}^{2}\leq O(\log^{2}n). We will show how 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} achieves this condition in Section 5.3.2.

5.3.2 Modified Global Interval Tree

In this section, we describe the data structure 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} for maintaining the blocking constraints {𝒥i,t}i∈[d]\{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\}_{i\in[d]}.

The idea is similar to 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}, but we include a full description here for completeness.

Similar to the interval representation in Section 3.2, the set of blocking-guarded prefixes 𝒥i,t\mathcal{J}_{i,t} (for row ii) corresponds naturally to consecutive intervals that partition [Wt][W_{t}]. We abuse notation and also use 𝒥i,t\mathcal{J}_{i,t} to denote the set of intervals in this partition. 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty} maintains these intervals {𝒥i,t}i∈[d]\{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\}_{i\in[d]} (that satisfy ∑i∈[d]|𝒥i,t|≤0.1​|Wt|\sum_{i\in[d]}|\mathcal{J}_{i,t}|\leq 0.1|W_{t}|) by adding and merging (small) intervals as before.

Initialization and Adding Intervals. Before the process starts, for each row i∈[d]i\in[d], we split [n][n] into a collection ℬi,0\mathcal{B}_{i,0} of base intervals, each with ℓ2\ell_{2}-squared mass s0=20​log⁡ns_{0}=20\log n.

Then, 𝒥i,0\mathcal{J}_{i,0} will be the set of all base intervals that are completely contained in the first 10​d10d columns.1515 15 We do not need an extra constraint at the end of the window as in Remark 3.2, since the entire time window WtW_{t} is blocked at each time step tt due to (4c).

Note that the total ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass of W0W_{0} over all dd rows is at most |W0||W_{0}| (as each column has ℓ2\ell_{2} norm at most 11), we have ∑i∈[d]|𝒥i,0|≤0.1​|W0|\sum_{i\in[d]}|\mathcal{J}_{i,0}|\leq 0.1|W_{0}|. As before, the data structure adds a base interval in ℬi,0\mathcal{B}_{i,0} to 𝒥i,t\mathcal{J}_{i,t} whenever it becomes active, i.e., it contains an active column and no dormant column.

Merging Intervals. Analogous to Section 3.2, the intervals in 𝒥i,t\mathcal{J}_{i,t} are merged using a global binary tree 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,t\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t}. Initially, 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,0\mathsf{Tree}_{i,0} is the complete binary tree of height O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) whose leaves correspond to all the base intervals ℬi,0\mathcal{B}_{i,0}, and at each time tt, 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,t\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} is a subtree of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,0\mathsf{Tree}_{i,0}. As before, the active leaves of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,t\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} correspond to intervals in 𝒥i,t\mathcal{J}_{i,t}.

As before, sibling leaves of 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,t\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} are merged carefully when they become small, defined as follows. The ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} size of an interval II in row ii at time tt is defined to be the ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass (in row ii) of the alive columns contained in II at time tt. We call an interval small if its ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} size is ≤s0/2=10​log⁡n\leq s_{0}/2=10\log n at time tt.

Analogous to Merging Rule 3.3, 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,t\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} is updated via the following merging rule.

Merging Rule 5.6 (Merging via 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty}).

At any time tt,

  1. 1.

    For any small left leaf v∈𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾tv\in\mathsf{Tree}_{t}, delete it and merge its interval with the interval at the next leaf; In particular, if the right sibling of vv is also a leaf, then also delete the right siblind and use their parent to represent the merged interval.

  2. 2.

    For any small right leaf v∈𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,tv\in\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t}, if their left sibling of vv has been deleted, then delete vv and use its parent to represent its interval.

We end this subsubsection by proving the correctness of 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty}. In Proposition 5.7, we bound the number of intervals in {𝒥i,t}i∈[d]\{\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\}_{i\in[d]} and in Proposition 5.8, we show that 𝖡𝖺𝖽i𝒫\mathsf{Bad}_{i}^{\mathcal{P}} has small ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass.

Proposition 5.7 (Number of blocking constraints).

At any time tt, consider 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,t\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} after Merging Rule 5.6 is completed. Then the average ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} size of active leaves in 𝖳𝗋𝖾𝖾i,t\mathsf{Tree}_{i,t} is at least s0/(2​log⁡n)=10s_{0}/(2\log n)=10. Consequently, the total number of blocking constraints is |∑i∈[d]𝒥i,t|≤0.1​|Wt|\big|\sum_{i\in[d]}\mathcal{J}_{i,t}\big|\leq 0.1|W_{t}|.

Proof.

The proof is essentially the same as the proof of Proposition 3.4. As before, there is no small left leaf. By the same charging argument there (that charges <log⁡n<\log n small right leaves to any active non-small left leaf), the average ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} size of the active leaves (or intervals in 𝒥i,t\mathcal{J}_{i,t}) is at least s0/(2​log⁡n)=10s_{0}/(2\log n)=10. The second statement in the proposition then follows immediately, by noting that the total ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} size of the time window WtW_{t} is at most |Wt||W_{t}|.

∎

Next we show how to bound the ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass of the bad set for 𝒫\mathcal{P} in row ii.

Proposition 5.8 (Bounding the bad set).

The ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass of 𝖡𝖺𝖽i𝒫\mathsf{Bad}^{\mathcal{P}}_{i} is at most (s/2)​log⁡n=O⁡(log2⁡n)(s/2)\log n=O(\log^{2}n).

Proof.

This proof is essentially the same as the proof of Proposition 3.6, by decomposing the prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} into a union of <log⁡n<\log n subtrees (for row ii), and show that each subtree contributes at most s/2s/2 to the ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass of 𝖡𝖺𝖽i𝒫\mathsf{Bad}^{\mathcal{P}}_{i}. We omit the details.

∎

5.3.3 Proof of Lemma 5.2

Now we are ready to complete the proof of Lemma 5.2.

Proof of Lemma 5.2.

Fix a prefix 𝒫\mathcal{P} and a row i∈[d]i\in[d]. Proposition 5.7 ensures that ∑i∈[d]|𝒥i,t|≤0.1​|Wt|\sum_{i\in[d]}|\mathcal{J}_{i,t}|\leq 0.1|W_{t}| at each time tt, so that the condition of Fact 3.1 is met and the algorithm is feasible. By Proposition 5.8, the ℓ22\ell_{2}^{2} mass of 𝖡𝖺𝖽i𝒫\mathsf{Bad}_{i}^{\mathcal{P}} is at most O⁡(log2⁡n)O(\log^{2}n). Then by [8, Theorem 1], with probability 1−1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(n)1-1/\mathsf{poly}(n), all time tt one has

|φt𝒫​(i)|≤O⁡(‖Ai​(𝖡𝖺𝖽i𝒫)‖22⋅log⁡n)≤O⁡(log3/2⁡n).|\varphi_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}(i)|\leq O\Big(\sqrt{\big\|A_{i}(\mathsf{Bad}_{i}^{\mathcal{P}})\big\|_{2}^{2}\cdot\log n}\Big)\leq O(\log^{3/2}n).

Taking a union bound over all prefixes 𝒫∈[n]\mathcal{P}\in[n] and rows i∈[d]i\in[d] completes the proof.

∎

6 Concluding Remarks

Our constructive bounds for ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy and Steinitz problems match the conjectured bounds when d≥𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀⁡(n)d\geq\mathsf{polylog}(n), where the 𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀\mathsf{polylog} factors are larger than those in Banaszczyk’s non-constructive results (where he only requires d≥log⁡nd\geq\log n). Below, we briefly explain the several reasons for this loss in our current analysis and mention some related open problems.

  1. (a)

    First, in the 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}} data structure, we lower bound the average interval size by Ω⁡(s/log⁡n)\Omega(s/\log n) (even though the base intervals have size ss), which results in an extra log⁡n\log n factor in the number of intervals we need to maintain; we also upper bound the size of the error set by O⁡(s​log⁡n)O(s\log n). Both these log⁡n\log n factors are due to the global binary tree having depth Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n). Nonetheless, as the sliding window has size |Wt|=O⁡(d)|W_{t}|=O(d), it may be possible to reduce these factors to log⁡d\log d if we could maintain a binary tree structure within WtW_{t}.

  2. (b)

    Second, as we are controlling γ𝖠𝖲𝖨=Θ~​(d)\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}=\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{d}) many ASI-guarded prefixes simultaneously, this leads to an extra Θ~​(d1/4)\widetilde{\Theta}(d^{1/4}) factor in the additive term (e.g., see (3)). Getting rid of this factor would require attaining O⁡(1)O(1)-affine spectral independence (or equivalently, satisfying (4f ASI) for only O⁡(1)O(1) prefixes), and it is unclear how to achieve this.

  3. (c)

    Third, we used the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy bound of O⁡(log3/2⁡n)O(\log^{3/2}n) in Lemma 5.2. The extra log⁡n\sqrt{\log n} loss (from the current best constructive bound of O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) in [2]) is due to the Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n) depth of 𝒯𝖦𝗅𝗈𝖻𝖺𝗅∞\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{Global}}^{\infty}, and it may be possible to replace it by a log⁡d\log d factor as mentioned in (a). Alternatively, it would be interesting to see if the (rather) different ideas in [2] could be combined with our algorithmic framework to achieve a O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) bound directly.

We now mention some open problems related to prefix discrepancy below.

Matching Banaszczyk’s Bound Algorithmically. It is an intriguing open question to match Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy.

Question 6.1 (Matching Banaszczyk’s bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy).

Given vectors v1,…,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥vi∥2≤1\lVert v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], does there exist an efficient algorithm that finds x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that ∥∑i=1txi​vi∥2≤O⁡(d+log⁡n)\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{\log n}) for all prefix t∈[n]t\in[n]?

Similarly, for the ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy (i.e., the prefix version of Komlós problem), it is widely open how to attain Banaszczyk’s O⁡(log⁡n)O(\sqrt{\log n}) bound algorithmically. As mentioned earlier, the current best algorithmic bound is O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) [2].

Question 6.2 (Matching Banaszczyk’s bound for prefix Komlós).

Given v1,v2,…​vn∈ℝdv_{1},v_{2},\ldots v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥vi∥2≤1\lVert v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], does there exist an efficient algorithm that can find x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that ∥∑i=1txi​vi∥∞≤O⁡(log⁡n)\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\rVert_{\infty}\leq O(\sqrt{\log n}) for all prefix t∈[n]t\in[n]?

More generally, any algorithm that can find a random coloring x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} such that every prefix discrepancy vector is O⁡(1)O(1)-subgaussian can attain both bounds above (in fact, this prefix O⁡(1)O(1)-subgaussian property is equivalent to Banaszczyk’s result in [5]). Currently, the best algorithm can only achieve O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-subgaussianity for every prefix discrepancy [2].

Beating Banaszczyk’s Bound for Prefix Discrepancy. For some time, one of the central goals of algorithmic discrepancy has been to match Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bound algorithmically. But recently, [11, 13] were able to go beyond and substantially improve upon Banaszczyk’s result for the Beck-Fiala and Komlós problems. It would be very interesting (and significant) to improve upon Banaszczyk’s non-constructive bounds for prefix discrepancy problems.

Question 6.3 (Beating Banaszczyk’s bound for ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} prefix discrepancy).

Given v1,…,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥vi∥2≤1\lVert v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], does there exist x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} with ∥∑i=1txi​vi∥2≤O⁡(d)+o⁡(log⁡n)\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq O(\sqrt{d})+o(\sqrt{\log n})?

Similarly, it is an open question to beat Banaszczyk’s O⁡(d​log⁡n)O(\sqrt{d\log n}) bound for the ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy problem. Interestingly, unlike the ℓ2\ell_{2} to ℓ2\ell_{2} setting, an algorithm matching Banaszczyk’s bound in this setting is known [8].

Question 6.4 (Beating Banaszczyk’s bound for ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} to ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} prefix discrepancy).

Given v1,…,vn∈ℝdv_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥vi∥∞≤1\lVert v_{i}\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1 for each i∈[n]i\in[n], does there exist x∈{±1}nx\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} with ∥∑i=1txi​vi∥∞≤o⁡(d​log⁡n)\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{t}x_{i}v_{i}\rVert_{\infty}\leq o(\sqrt{d\log n})?

Another closely related question is Tusnády’s problem, which asks for the combinatorial discrepancy of all axis-parallel rectangles for an arbitrary set of nn points in [0,1]d[0,1]^{d}. For this problem, the current best lower bound is Ω⁡(logd−1⁡n)\Omega(\log^{d-1}n) [45], while the current best non-constructive bound (which crucially relies on Banaszczyk’s result) is O⁡(logd−1/2⁡n)O(\log^{d-1/2}n) [47], and the current best constructive bound is O⁡(logd⁡n)O(\log^{d}n) [8]. It would be quite interesting to improve any of these results.

Appendix A SDP Feasibility

In this subsection, we give the statement of the SDP feasibility theorem in [13, Theorem A.4] and explain how Fact 3.1 follows from it.

Theorem A.1 (Theorem A.4 of [13]).

Let W⊂ℝhW\subset\mathbb{R}^{h} be a subspace with dimension dim⁡(W)=δ​h,\mathrm{dim}(W)=\delta h, and Es∈ℝrs​h×hE_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{s}h\times h} for all s∈[q]s\in[q] be a set of matrices with rs≥1r_{s}\geq 1. Then, for any 0≤κ,η,ηs<10\leq\kappa,\eta,\eta_{s}<1, where s∈[q]s\in[q], such that η+κ+∑s=1qηs≤1−δ\eta+\kappa+\sum_{s=1}^{q}\eta_{s}\leq 1-\delta, there is an h×hh\times h PSD matrix UU satisfying:

  1. 1.

    Uj,j≤1U_{j,j}\leq 1 for all j∈[h]j\in[h],

  2. 2.

    Tr⁡(U)≥κ​h\mathrm{Tr}(U)\geq\kappa h,

  3. 3.

    ⟨w​w⊤,U⟩\langle ww^{\top},U\rangle for all w∈Ww\in W,

  4. 4.

    U⪯1η​𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀​(U)U\preceq\frac{1}{\eta}\mathsf{diag}(U), and

  5. 5.

    Es​U​Es⊤⪯rsηs​𝖽𝗂𝖺𝗀​(Es​U​Es⊤)E_{s}UE_{s}^{\top}\preceq\frac{r_{s}}{\eta_{s}}\mathsf{diag}(E_{s}UE_{s}^{\top}) for all s∈[q]s\in[q].

Furthermore, such a PSD matrix UU can be computed by solving a semidefinite program (SDP).

To obtain Fact 3.1 from Theorem A.1, we set the parameters in Theorem A.1 for our SDP (4) as follows. We set κ=0.1\kappa=0.1 corresponding to the trace condition in (4b).

Blocking Constraints. The subspace WW in Theorem A.1 will contain the subspace HtH_{t} for the blocking constraints in (4c), which has dim(Ht)≤0.1​|Wt|\dim(H_{t})\leq 0.1|W_{t}|, as well as the dd rows of the sliding window WtW_{t} provided |Wt|=10​d|W_{t}|=10d (as mentioned in Footnote 11, if |Wt|<10​d|W_{t}|<10d, the constraint (4d) will be dropped).

This corresponds to setting δ\delta to be at most 0.20.2 in Theorem A.1.

SI Constraint. The SI constraint (4e SI) corresponds to setting η=0.1\eta=0.1 in Theorem A.1.

ASI Constraint. The constraint (4f ASI) corresponds to setting q=1q=1 and η1=0.1\eta_{1}=0.1 in Theorem A.1, as the ratio between the row and column dimensions of EtE_{t} is r1=0.1​γ𝖠𝖲𝖨r_{1}=0.1\gamma_{\mathsf{ASI}}.

The parameter setting above clearly satisfies κ+δ+η+η1<1\kappa+\delta+\eta+\eta_{1}<1, and thus Theorem A.1 implies the feasibility of our SDP (4) and hence Fact 3.1.
